name: Sumerian city-states
summary: In the marshy south of Mesopotamia, Uruk and its neighbours grew into the world's first cities and, by c. 3300 BCE, the first writing. Through the Early Dynastic period (c. 2900–2334 BCE) rival city-states such as Kish, Ur, Lagash and Umma fought over land and water, until Lugalzagesi united Sumer, only to lose it to Sargon of Akkad. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).

events.text: Late Uruk period: Uruk is the leading city of southern Mesopotamia
events.detail: In the fourth millennium BCE, farming villages on the irrigated plains of southern Mesopotamia grew into the first true cities, and Uruk outgrew them all. In the Late Uruk period it covered roughly 230–250 hectares, with monumental buildings in its Eanna district and perhaps 25,000–50,000 inhabitants, far more than any rival settlement. Uruk-style outposts and colonies, such as the walled town of Habuba Kabira, spread up the Euphrates into Syria. This 'Uruk expansion' made southern Mesopotamia, the heart of the map's Sumerian territory, the most urban and influential region of the Near East.

events.text: Earliest unequivocal written documents (proto-cuneiform) appear at Uruk
events.detail: Running a city of thousands meant keeping track of grain, livestock, labour and rations, and for a long time clay tokens had been used for counting. From about 3300 BCE, in the phase archaeologists call Uruk IV, scribes at Uruk began drawing signs and numbers on clay tablets with a reed stylus: the earliest unequivocal written documents. Almost all of them are administrative records, not stories or laws. Writing gave Sumer's temples and rulers a powerful tool for managing people and goods, and its descendant, cuneiform, would be used across the Near East for more than 3,000 years.

events.text: Jemdet Nasr period: writing becomes more abstract; cities run central administrations
events.detail: After the Uruk expansion faded, the period named after the site of Jemdet Nasr (c. 3100–2900 BCE) saw southern culture continue on a more local scale, limited to south-central Iraq. Writing kept developing: pictures gave way to simpler, more abstract signs, and the script began to take on its wedge-shaped look. Tablets, cylinder seals and large central buildings suggest that a central administration rationed food and organised crafts and farming. A seal impression listing cities such as Ur, Uruk and Larsa hints at close ties between them, the network from which Sumer's city-states would emerge.

events.text: Early Dynastic period begins: rival city-states ruled by kings (lugal)
events.detail: From about 2900 BCE southern Mesopotamia was divided among independent city-states, each a large city controlling the surrounding villages, fields and canals, and each protected by its own god. The most important included Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Adab and Umma, while Kish in the north may have led a larger territorial state. Rulers bore titles such as ensi (governor) or lugal (literally 'big man', meaning king). Because these rival states competed for land and irrigation water, the map shows Sumer as a cluster of cities rather than a single kingdom for the next five centuries.

events.text: Era of Gilgamesh of Uruk and Enmebaragesi of Kish, kings of later legend
events.detail: The early centuries of the Early Dynastic period left almost no contemporary texts, so they are known mainly through later legend. Enmebaragesi of Kish is the earliest king on the Sumerian King List whose name has been found in inscriptions; scholars date him to c. 2700–2600 BCE. Gilgamesh of Uruk was probably a real king of roughly the same era, and a Sumerian poem tells of his revolt against Enmebaragesi's son Agga of Kish. Later generations made Gilgamesh a god and the hero of a famous epic, but the real political map of this 'heroic age' cannot be reconstructed.

events.text: Royal Cemetery of Ur: rich burials with goods traded from the Indus
events.detail: By the 26th century BCE Ur was among the richest cities of Sumer. Its cemetery, excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s, held about 2,000 burials, including sixteen 'royal' tombs in which rulers such as Queen Puabi were buried with attendants, sometimes seventy or more. The graves were filled with gold, silver, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan and carnelian beads that point to trade with the Indus Valley. These treasures show that Sumer, which had to import all its metals, sat at the centre of a trade network reaching from the Gulf to Afghanistan and India.

events.text: Mesilim of Kish arbitrates the border war between Lagash and Umma
events.detail: Lagash and its neighbour Umma were locked in a long quarrel over the Gu-Edin, a fertile irrigated plain on their shared border. Around the middle of the third millennium (c. 2550 BCE by one estimate), Mesilim, king of Kish, who seems to have held some authority over Lagash and Adab, stepped in as arbiter. Claiming the guidance of the god Ishtaran, he fixed a new boundary and set up an inscribed pillar to mark it. The settlement did not last: a later king of Umma, Ush, tore the pillar down, and the border war flared again for generations.

events.text: Eannatum of Lagash defeats Umma; Stele of the Vultures
events.detail: Eannatum of Lagash, grandson of the dynasty's founder Ur-Nanshe, renewed the war for the Gu-Edin. Around 2450 BCE he defeated Ush of Umma, whose army, according to Eannatum's inscription, left 3,600 dead, and then imposed a boundary treaty and grain payments on Umma's next ruler, Enakalle. He celebrated the victory on the Stele of the Vultures, named after the birds shown carrying off enemy heads; its fragments are now in the Louvre. Eannatum also fought Ur, Uruk, Kish, Mari and parts of Elam, making Lagash briefly the strongest power in Sumer, though revolts soon followed.

events.text: Urukagina rules Lagash; Lugalzagesi of Umma conquers Uruk
events.detail: Urukagina (also read Uruinimgina) became ruler of Lagash after Lugalanda and is famous for inscriptions listing changes he made, such as cutting the fees officials charged for burials. Historians now doubt there was one coherent 'reform', and many lines of the texts are hard to interpret. Meanwhile Umma, Lagash's old rival, expanded under Lugalzagesi, who took Uruk in the seventh year of his reign. Lugalzagesi then ravaged Lagash and its temples, leaving Urukagina to rule only from Girsu, and the balance of power in Sumer shifted to Umma and Uruk.

events.text: Lugalzagesi rules all Sumer from Uruk, the first such kingdom on record
events.detail: Having crushed Lagash, Lugalzagesi overthrew the king of Kish and took Ur, Nippur and Larsa, making Uruk his capital. His inscriptions call him 'king of the Land' and claim that the god Enlil gave him all the lands from the Lower Sea (the Gulf) to the Upper Sea (the Mediterranean), though his westward reach may have been little more than a raid. He is the first ruler reliably documented to have united all of Sumer in one kingdom, which the Sumerian King List says lasted 25 years. For a generation the map's many city-states became a single realm centred on Uruk.

events.text: Sargon of Akkad comes to power; Lugalzagesi's kingdom falls to him
events.detail: Sargon built his power at Akkad, a city in central Mesopotamia whose site has never been found; later legend says he had begun as cupbearer to the king of Kish. Lugalzagesi's kingdom now faced this new northern rival. According to Sargon's own inscriptions, three battles were needed to defeat Lugalzagesi; Sargon tore down Uruk's walls and led the captured king in a neck-stock to Enlil's temple at Nippur. The date is debated: Sargon's reign is usually placed from c. 2334 BCE, but the conquest of Sumer is often dated nearer 2300. Sumer's age of independent city-states was over.

name: Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad (r. c. 2334–2279 BCE) conquered Sumer and campaigned from the Gulf to Syria and Elam, creating the first empire to rule all Mesopotamia. His grandson Naram-Sin crushed a great revolt and took the realm to its widest extent, but after Shar-kali-sharri (d. c. 2193 BCE) the state broke apart under Gutian and Amorite pressure and fell c. 2154 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Sargon comes to power and founds a dynasty ruling from Akkad (site still unknown)
events.detail: Sargon emerged as ruler of Akkad, a small city in central Mesopotamia whose exact site is still unknown; it probably lay near where the Tigris meets the Adhem or Diyala rivers. Almost nothing reliable is known about his rise. Legends written long afterwards call him a usurper who began as cupbearer to King Ur-Zababa of Kish, and some historians suspect he was a vassal of Kish who rebelled. His reign is usually dated c. 2334–2279 BCE, though other estimates run 2316–2277. For perhaps 18 years or more his power seems to have been limited to the north.

events.text: Sargon defeats Lugalzagesi in three battles, razes Uruk's walls and takes Sumer
events.detail: The turning point of Sargon's career was his clash with Lugalzagesi, who ruled a united Sumer from Uruk. According to Sargon's inscriptions, three battles were needed to defeat Lugalzagesi and his allies; Sargon 'conquered fifty governors', razed Uruk's walls and led the captured king in a neck-stock to Enlil's temple at Nippur. The date is debated but is usually put around 2300 BCE. Sumer's cities became provinces under governors, some of them 'sons of Akkad', and for the first time the whole of southern Mesopotamia answered to a single king.

events.text: Sargon takes Mari and claims the 'Upper Country' to the Cedar Forest
events.detail: With Sumer secured, Sargon turned to Syria, then dominated by Mari on the middle Euphrates, Nagar and Ebla. One of his year-names records the destruction of Mari, and an inscription says the god Dagan at Tuttul gave him 'the Upper Land: Mari, Yarmuti and Ebla as far as the Cedar Forest and the Silver Mountains'. Sargon also boasted of 34 victorious battles and of ships from Dilmun, Magan and Meluhha docking at Akkad. These campaigns stretched Akkad's reach towards the Mediterranean and the Taurus, though how firmly the west was held is uncertain, and the date here is approximate.

events.text: Sargon dies; Rimush reconquers rebel cities including Ur, Umma and Lagash
events.detail: Sargon died c. 2279 BCE (other estimates are 2284 or 2277), and his son Rimush inherited an empire whose conquered cities still remembered independence. Rimush's inscriptions describe widespread revolts and the reconquest of Ur, Umma, Adab, Lagash, Der and Kazallu, claiming tens of thousands of enemies killed or captured. He also campaigned east against Elam and Marhashi. His reign was short, about nine years according to the Sumerian King List, and a later tradition says his own courtiers killed him. Still, he held Sargon's empire together and kept Sumer within its borders.

events.text: Manishtushu leads a fleet down the Gulf against 32 kings; takes Anshan
events.detail: Rimush's brother Manishtushu became king c. 2270 BCE and, free of the revolts that had troubled his brother, looked outward. According to his inscription, he sent ships across the 'Lower Sea' (the Persian Gulf), defeated an alliance of 32 cities on the far shore, plundered as far as the silver mines, and brought back black stone for a statue of himself. He also conquered Anshan in Elam, and Akkadian governors came to rule Elam and Pashime on the Iranian coast. He died c. 2255 BCE after about fifteen years, possibly murdered by his courtiers, with Akkad's grip on south-western Iran tightened.

events.text: Naram-Sin succeeds; under him the empire reaches its greatest extent
events.detail: Naram-Sin, Manishtushu's son and Sargon's grandson, ruled c. 2255–2218 BCE, and under him the Akkadian state reached its greatest extent. He defeated the ruler of Magan, fought hill peoples of the Zagros, Taurus and Amanus mountains, and destroyed Armanum and Ebla in Syria, claiming the Amanus, the 'Cedar Mountain' and the Upper Sea. He was the first king to call himself 'King of the Four Quarters', meaning ruler of the whole world. On the map, Akkad's power now stretched from the Gulf and western Iran to northern Syria and the Mediterranean coast.

events.text: Victory Stele: Naram-Sin defeats the Lullubi of the Zagros
events.detail: The Lullubi were a mountain people of the Zagros, astride routes between Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau. Naram-Sin's army defeated them and their chief Satuni, a victory celebrated on a 2-metre stele of pinkish limestone dated only to his reign. Breaking with older art, it shows the battle climbing diagonally up a mountain, with Naram-Sin at the top wearing a horned helmet, a sign of divinity. Victories like this carried Akkad's power into the Zagros on the empire's eastern edge. Over a thousand years later the Elamite king Shutruk-Nakhunte carried the stele off to Susa; it is now in the Louvre.

events.text: Naram-Sin crushes the Great Revolt and is proclaimed a god
events.detail: At an uncertain point in Naram-Sin's reign, a huge coalition rose against Akkad, led by Iphur-Kish of Kish and Amar-Girid of Uruk and joined by Nippur, Sippar, Kutha, Borsippa and other cities, as well as Amorite highlanders. Naram-Sin claimed that he won nine battles in a single year and captured the kings the rebels had raised. Afterwards, his inscription says, the people of Akkad asked the great gods to make him the god of their city. He became the first Mesopotamian king to claim divinity, and the empire came through intact.

events.text: Shar-kali-sharri succeeds; wars with Gutians, Amorites and Elam
events.detail: Naram-Sin's son Shar-kali-sharri reigned for about 25 years (c. 2218–2193 BCE). His year-names suggest a fairly peaceful reign with recurring clashes: a victory over the Amorites (MAR.TU) at Jebel Bishri in Syria, the capture of a Gutian king, and a battle against Elam and Zahara near Akshak. Economic texts suggest reasonable prosperity. Yet the Gutians were growing stronger and at some point made Adab, in Sumer, their capital. Later tradition held that the empire began to unravel during his reign, as outsiders and restless provinces tested Akkad's strength.

events.text: Shar-kali-sharri dies; anarchy: 'Who was king? Who was not the king?'
events.detail: When Shar-kali-sharri died c. 2193 BCE, no successor could hold the empire together. The Sumerian King List sums up the chaos with a famous question, 'Then who was king? Who was not the king?', naming four rivals, Igigi, Imi, Nanum and Ilulu, who together ruled only three years. Southern cities such as Lagash and Uruk began to reassert their independence, while Gutians, Amorites and Elamites pressed in. Many historians also link the collapse to a severe drought, the '4.2-kiloyear event', that struck Upper Mesopotamia, as Akkad's territory shrank back towards its northern core.

events.text: Reign of Shu-turul ends; Akkad's empire is gone as Gutians dominate
events.detail: After the anarchy, Dudu and then his son Shu-turul ruled a much-reduced kingdom of Akkad in northern Babylonia, including Kish, Tutub, Nippur and Eshnunna. Shu-turul, said to have reigned 15 years, is known only from a few seals and votive objects. With his death c. 2154 BCE the Sumerian King List says kingship passed to Uruk, while the Gutians, based at Adab, became the main regional power and southern cities such as Ur and Lagash ruled themselves. The first empire in Mesopotamian history disappeared from the map, but Sargon and Naram-Sin remained models for later kings.

name: Third Dynasty of Ur (Neo-Sumerian Empire)
summary: After the Gutian interlude, Ur-Nammu of Ur (r. c. 2112–2094 BCE) reunited Sumer and Akkad, and his son Shulgi built a centralised, bureaucratic state of some twenty provinces ringed by a military periphery along the Zagros. Amorite incursions, revolts and the breakaway of Isin weakened his successors, and c. 2004 BCE an Elamite coalition sacked Ur. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Ur-Nammu takes power at Ur and founds the Third Dynasty
events.detail: After Akkad fell, Sumer was split between Gutian rulers and revived city-states, until Utu-hengal of Uruk defeated the Gutian king Tirigan. Ur-Nammu, who had governed Ur and may have been Utu-hengal's brother, then took power himself c. 2112 BCE, defeated his former masters at Uruk and conquered Lagash. Taking the title 'King of Sumer and Akkad', he reunited southern Mesopotamia, restored temples and canals, and began the Great Ziggurat of Ur. The oldest surviving law collection, the Code of Ur-Nammu, is linked to him or his son. Sumer was once again a single kingdom, now ruled from Ur.

events.text: Ur-Nammu dies in battle in the eastern highlands; Shulgi begins a 48-year reign
events.detail: Ur-Nammu pushed his rule north-east towards the Diyala valley, probably defeating the Elamite king Puzur-Inshushinak along the way. After about 18 years on the throne he died on the battlefield in the eastern highlands; a later poem, the 'Death of Ur-Nammu', mourns him, and some read it as saying his army abandoned him. His son Shulgi succeeded c. 2094 BCE and reigned for about 48 years, roughly half the life of the whole dynasty. Shulgi would turn his father's kingdom into an empire on the model of Akkad, although his first twenty years are known mostly from temple-building.

events.text: Shulgi, a god by his 21st year, reforms weights, taxes and the bureaucracy
events.detail: Around the middle of his reign Shulgi carried out reforms that reshaped the state, though some may have begun under his father and few can be dated exactly. He reorganised the army, standardised weights and measures, reformed writing and the scribal schools, and unified taxes, including the bala system in which each province took turns supplying the centre. A huge livestock and administrative hub was built at Puzrish-Dagan near Nippur. By his 21st year, and perhaps as early as his 12th, Shulgi had proclaimed himself a god. The result looked like a highly centralised state, at least in its Sumerian core.

events.text: Shulgi destroys Simurrum: first of many campaigns in the Zagros
events.detail: Shulgi's later reign was dominated by wars in the Zagros foothills and along the upper Tigris, lands rich in pasture and trade routes. His 25th year-name records the destruction of Simurrum, a mountain kingdom north of the Diyala; later names boast of destroying it a second, a third and eventually a ninth time, showing how hard such enemies were to hold down. Conquered districts became a defensive, tribute-paying periphery with garrisons and military colonies, rather like the Roman frontier. On the map, Ur's power now reached north-east from Sumer towards the Zagros.

events.text: Shulgi's daughter marries the governor of Anshan in Elam
events.detail: Alongside war, Shulgi used marriage diplomacy with the kingdoms of the Iranian plateau. In his 18th year a daughter became queen of Marhashi, and the name for his 30th year records that the governor of Anshan, in Elam, married another daughter; others married rulers of Pashime. Such ties did not guarantee peace: by his 34th year Shulgi was campaigning against Anshan, and a year-name records its destruction. The kings of Ur also controlled Susa, where Shulgi built temples, so Elam's western lowlands were drawn firmly into Ur's orbit.

events.text: Shulgi builds a wall to keep out Tidnum (Amorite) nomads
events.detail: Amorites (Martu), Semitic-speaking groups from Syria and Upper Mesopotamia often described as tribal and nomadic, had been moving into southern Mesopotamia since late Akkadian times. In his 37th year Shulgi built 'the wall of the land' in the north of Akkad to keep out the Tidnum, an Amorite group. The wall marked the empire's north-western frontier and showed that pressure from the steppe had become a lasting worry. His successors had to reinforce it, and Amorite incursions eventually played a major part in the empire's collapse.

events.text: One campaign defeats Urbilum, Simurrum, Lullubum and Karhar
events.detail: The climax of Shulgi's wars came near the end of his reign. The name for his 45th year boasts that he 'smashed the heads of Urbilum, Simurrum, Lullubum and Karhar in a single campaign'. Urbilum is Arbela (modern Erbil in northern Iraq), and the other lands lay in the Zagros foothills; around the same time he destroyed Kimash and Hurtum near Elam. These victories pushed Ur's ring of tribute-paying border lands to its widest, stretching along the Tigris and the Zagros from Urbilum to Susa, and made Ur the leading power of Mesopotamia.

events.text: Shu-Sin succeeds and builds a new wall against Amorite incursions
events.detail: After Shulgi died, his son Amar-Sin reigned about nine years, followed by Amar-Sin's brother Shu-Sin (c. 2037–2029 BCE). Shu-Sin had to reassert control in the northern and eastern borderlands, where tribute was arriving less regularly, a sign that Ur's grip was loosening. The most threatening danger came from Amorites in the north-west, and after an open revolt he built a new fortified wall between the Euphrates and the Tigris, strengthening Shulgi's defences. Late in his reign much real power lay with his chancellor Aradmu. The borders held for now, but the outer lands were slipping.

events.text: Ibbi-Sin succeeds; within three years the central archives dry up
events.detail: Ibbi-Sin, probably Shu-Sin's son, came to the throne c. 2028 BCE and reigned for 24 years while the empire fell apart. The archives of the main administrative centres in the heartland dry up after his third year, a sign that the central bureaucracy had lost control of the provinces. Eastern lands such as Anshan and Susa broke away, Eshnunna became independent, and Amorite raids grew more violent. In his seventh and eighth years the price of grain rose to some 60 times normal, pointing to famine. On the map, Ur's empire shrank towards the city of Ur itself.

events.text: Ishbi-Erra holds Isin under his own year-names, breaking from Ur
events.detail: Ishbi-Erra, an official described as a 'man of Mari', had been sent by Ibbi-Sin to buy grain at Isin and Kazallu. According to letters preserved as later school exercises, whose authenticity is uncertain, he complained that Amorite raids stopped him shipping it and asked to be made governor of Isin and Nippur. By Ibbi-Sin's eighth year he was dating documents by his own year-names, in effect declaring independence at Isin. His power grew as Ibbi-Sin's declined, splitting the former empire in two, and his dynasty of Isin would later present itself as Ur's heir.

events.text: Elamites under Kindattu sack Ur, ending the dynasty
events.detail: By the end Ibbi-Sin held little beyond the city of Ur. Around 2004 BCE (middle chronology) an army from Elam and the Shimashki highlands of the Zagros, led by King Kindattu, sacked Ur and carried Ibbi-Sin off in chains to Elam, where he died. The disaster was remembered in the 'Lament for Sumer and Ur', which describes the city reduced to ruin mounds. The Elamites occupied Ur until Ishbi-Erra of Isin drove them out. The fall of Ur ended the last great Sumerian state, and Mesopotamia split into rival Amorite-led kingdoms such as Isin and Larsa.

name: Old Babylonian Empire (Hammurabi)
summary: Hammurabi (r. c. 1792–1750 BCE) turned Babylon from one Amorite kingdom among many into the master of Mesopotamia, conquering Larsa, Mari and Eshnunna and issuing his famous law code. Under his son Samsu-iluna revolts wrecked the southern cities and the far south broke away as the Sealand dynasty; a shrunken kingdom lasted until the Hittite king Mursili I sacked Babylon c. 1595 BCE. Dates follow the middle chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Hammurabi succeeds Sin-muballit as king of Babylon
events.detail: Since the fall of Ur, Mesopotamia had been divided among kingdoms ruled by Amorite dynasties. Babylon was a secondary city where an Amorite dynasty had taken root about a century earlier and built a modest kingdom including Kish, Sippar and Borsippa. When Hammurabi succeeded his father Sin-muballit in 1792 BCE (middle chronology), he was surrounded by stronger neighbours: Rim-Sin's Larsa in the south, Eshnunna in the Diyala valley, and Shamshi-Adad's kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia, with whom Babylon kept good relations. For two decades he mostly built temples and canals.

events.text: Hammurabi conquers Larsa and annexes Rim-Sin's kingdom in the south
events.detail: After helping to repel an Elamite invasion of Mesopotamia, Hammurabi turned on Rim-Sin of Larsa, the long-reigning king who had earlier absorbed Isin and Uruk. Citing Rim-Sin's poor support against Elam and alleged raids, he launched a lightning war with help from his ally Zimri-Lim of Mari. Larsa was besieged until its defenders ran short of food; Babylonian troops took the walls and brought Rim-Sin out alive. With Larsa annexed in 1763 BCE (some accounts say 1764), Hammurabi controlled all of southern Mesopotamia and took the old title 'king of Sumer and Akkad'.

events.text: Hammurabi takes Mari on the Euphrates; its palace is destroyed by 1759
events.detail: Mari, on the middle Euphrates, was a rich trading kingdom whose palace archives of more than 25,000 tablets are a key source for this age. Its king Zimri-Lim had been Hammurabi's ally, but the two fell out, apparently over Babylonian ambitions in the Jebel Sinjar region. The course of the war is not recorded, but the outcome is clear: Mari was captured around 1761 BCE and destroyed by 1759, ending its archive. Babylon now controlled the Euphrates route towards Syria, and the map's Babylonian realm stretched far upstream.

events.text: Ekallatum in Assyria is subjugated; Eshnunna has already been beaten
events.detail: North of Babylon, Eshnunna in the Diyala valley had been weakened by the Elamite war. Hammurabi first allied with its new king, Silli-Sin, who married one of his daughters, but then defeated it, a victory named in his 32nd year. The name for his next year boasts that he subjugated Mari and 'the many cities of Subartu', including Ekallatum on the Tigris, once the seat of Shamshi-Adad's son Ishme-Dagan, and Assyria was reduced to a vassal. Babylon was now master of almost all Mesopotamia, from the Gulf to the upper Tigris.

events.text: Code of Hammurabi set up late in his reign
events.detail: Near the end of his reign, Hammurabi had his laws inscribed on stone monuments. The best-preserved copy is a basalt stele 2.25 metres tall, topped by a relief of the king before Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. Its prologue says the gods chose him 'to prevent the strong from oppressing the weak', and its rulings, written as 'if this, then that' cases, cover crime, family, property and trade, including 'an eye for an eye'. The exact date is uncertain (often c. 1753 BCE). Taken to Susa as Elamite plunder centuries later, the stele was found in 1901 and is now in the Louvre.

events.text: Hammurabi dies; his son Samsu-iluna succeeds
events.detail: Hammurabi died around 1750 BCE, in the 43rd year of his reign, apparently after a long illness; his son Samsu-iluna seems to have been running the kingdom in his final months. In four decades Hammurabi had turned Babylon from one Amorite kingdom among many into the master of Mesopotamia, and the city would remain the region's leading centre for over a thousand years. But his empire had been won by conquest within a single lifetime, and many newly conquered cities still remembered independence. Samsu-iluna inherited a realm that would soon start to shrink.

events.text: Rim-Sin II's revolt spreads to 26 cities; first known Kassite attack repelled
events.detail: In Samsu-iluna's ninth year (c. 1741 BCE), a man calling himself Rim-Sin, perhaps a nephew of the king Hammurabi had defeated, led a revolt from Larsa. It spread to some 26 cities, including Uruk, Ur and Isin in the south and Eshnunna in the north. Within a year Samsu-iluna broke the northern rebels and had the king of Eshnunna executed. That same year he turned back an invading Kassite army, the earliest known mention of the people who would later rule Babylonia. The kingdom survived the shock, but the south remained at war.

events.text: Samsu-iluna retakes Larsa; Ur and Uruk sacked, the south largely abandoned
events.detail: For several years Samsu-iluna's armies fought Rim-Sin II's forces across the borderlands between Babylon, Sumer and Elam. Eventually he attacked Ur, pulled down its walls and sacked it, then did the same to Uruk and Isin, before finally defeating Larsa. Records from Ur and Uruk stop after his tenth year, and archaeology suggests these ancient cities were largely abandoned for centuries, until well into the Kassite period. Whether war alone was to blame, or Samsu-iluna made a deliberate retreat, is debated, but the old Sumerian south of the map was emptied.

events.text: Ilum-ma-ili's revolt founds the Sealand dynasty; Sumer lost for centuries
events.detail: A few years later a new pretender, Ilum-ma-ili, claiming descent from the last king of Isin, raised another revolt across Sumer. After an indecisive first battle, he defeated Samsu-iluna in a second and founded the First Sealand Dynasty in the far south. Samsu-iluna turned to defence, rebuilding fortresses around Nippur, while Assyria and Elam also broke free of Babylon. The south stayed independent for roughly 270–300 years (estimates differ), and the Babylonian kingdom shrank back towards its northern core around Babylon and the middle Euphrates.

events.text: Mursili I of Hatti sacks Babylon, ending Hammurabi's dynasty
events.detail: Hammurabi's successors ruled a much smaller kingdom: Abi-eshuh failed to retake the Sealand, and the last king, Samsu-ditana, faced growing pressure from the Kassites. Then, around 1595 BCE (middle chronology; proposed dates vary by as much as 230 years), the Hittite king Mursili I marched some 2,000 kilometres from Anatolia, destroyed Aleppo and sacked Babylon, carrying captives and treasure back to Hattusa. The Hittites did not stay. Their raid ended Hammurabi's dynasty, which had ruled Babylon for about three centuries, and the Kassites took control of Babylonia for the next four centuries.

name: Hittite Empire
summary: From their capital Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittite kings Hattusili I and Mursili I raided as far as Aleppo and Babylon (c. 1595 BCE) before the Old Kingdom sank into court strife. Suppiluliuma I (c. 1350–1322 BCE) broke Mitanni and made the Hittites masters of Syria; his successors fought Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and made peace. Around 1190 BCE, amid the wider Bronze Age collapse, Hattusa was abandoned and the empire vanished. All dates are approximate (middle chronology).

events.text: Hattusili I (or Labarna) founds the kingdom with Hattusa as capital
events.detail: The Hittites, speakers of an Indo-European language, had formed small kingdoms in central Anatolia around Kussara and Kanesh. Around 1650 BCE (middle chronology), Hattusili I, who may also have used the name Labarna, moved the capital from Nesha (Kanesh) to Hattusa, inside the great bend of the Kizilirmak (Halys) river, and took his throne name from it. His annals describe campaigns against Arzawa in the west and into northern Syria, where he attacked but did not take Aleppo, and a crossing of the Euphrates. Central Anatolia became the core of a kingdom that would last over four centuries.

events.text: Mursili I raids Aleppo and sacks Babylon
events.detail: Hattusili's grandson and chosen heir, Mursili I, renewed the wars in Syria. He destroyed Aleppo, capital of the kingdom of Yamhad, which had resisted his grandfather, then led an unprecedented march of some 2,000 kilometres down the Euphrates and sacked Babylon around 1595 BCE, ending Hammurabi's dynasty. Babylonia was far too distant to hold and passed to the Kassites. Back home, Mursili was murdered by his brother-in-law Hantili. Decades of royal murders followed, the Hurrians seized Aleppo and the south-eastern coast, and the Hittite realm shrank back towards central Anatolia.

events.text: Telipinu's reign closes the Old Kingdom after years of internal strife
events.detail: By the time Telipinu took the throne (c. 1525 BCE), murders and coups had shaken the royal family, and the kingdom had lost its conquests to Arzawa in the west, Mitanni in the east, the Kaska in the north and Kizzuwatna in the south. Telipinu won back some ground by allying with Kizzuwatna. He is best known for the Edict of Telipinu, which set out who should inherit the throne (first-rank sons, then lesser sons, then the husband of a first-rank daughter) to end the bloodshed. After him the Hittites entered a poorly recorded 'Middle Kingdom' of about seventy years.

events.text: Suppiluliuma I takes Aleppo and overruns Mitanni's capital Washukanni
events.detail: After a long period of weakness and invasion, the Hittites recovered under Suppiluliuma I (c. 1350–1322 BCE), a successful general who seized the throne after supporters murdered the young heir Tudhaliya. His great rival was Mitanni, the Hurrian kingdom of northern Mesopotamia. In the so-called One-Year War he overran Mitanni's vassals, captured and plundered its capital Washukanni, and crossed into Syria, taking Aleppo, Alalakh, Qatna and other small kingdoms, while Ugarit became his ally. Mitanni was broken, and the map's Hittite realm now spread from Anatolia deep into northern Syria.

events.text: Carchemish captured; Egypt's widowed queen asks him for a son to wed
events.detail: The last Mitannian stronghold west of the Euphrates was Carchemish. While besieging it, Suppiluliuma received an astonishing letter from Egypt's widowed queen, most likely Tutankhamun's widow Ankhesenamun: she had no son and asked for one of his sons to marry, so that he would become king of Egypt. After some hesitation he sent his son Zannanza, who was killed on the way. Carchemish fell, and Suppiluliuma made his sons viceroys at Carchemish and Aleppo to rule Hittite Syria. Blaming Egypt for Zannanza's death, he attacked Egyptian territory, opening a long period of hostility.

events.text: Suppiluliuma I dies of a plague that ravages Hatti for two decades
events.detail: Suppiluliuma's revenge raids into Egyptian territory brought back prisoners of war, and according to the 'Plague Prayers' of his son Mursili II, those prisoners carried an epidemic into Hatti. People went on dying for at least two decades; some historians suggest the disease was tularaemia. It is often considered the cause of Suppiluliuma's death c. 1322 BCE and of his eldest son and successor, Arnuwanda II, soon afterwards. Mursili II inherited a strong position in Syria but a stricken homeland, and blamed the gods' anger on his father's broken oaths.

events.text: Muwatalli II fights Ramesses II at Kadesh
events.detail: Egypt's new 19th Dynasty wanted to win back Syria, and Ramesses II invaded Amurru, a borderland both powers claimed. In May 1274 BCE (by the usual chronology), the Hittite king Muwatalli II ambushed the Egyptian army near Kadesh on the Orontes, after sending spies to mislead Ramesses. Some 5,000–6,000 chariots may have taken part, probably the largest chariot battle ever fought. Ramesses rallied his troops and reinforcements drove off the Hittites, but the battle ended in stalemate. Ramesses withdrew, while Muwatalli went on to seize the Egyptian province of Upi around Damascus, keeping Syria Hittite.

events.text: Hattusili III and Ramesses II make a peace treaty
events.detail: After Muwatalli's death, his son Urhi-Teshub (Mursili III) was overthrown by his uncle Hattusili III, who wanted foreign recognition, while Assyria was seizing the former lands of Mitanni and threatening both empires. Around 1259 BCE, in Ramesses II's 21st year, the two powers agreed the 'Eternal Treaty', the oldest known surviving peace treaty, preserved in both an Egyptian version and Akkadian tablets from Hattusa. Each side promised not to invade the other, to help against attackers or rebels, and to return political refugees. A Hittite princess later married Ramesses, and the Syrian frontier stayed fixed.

events.text: Suppiluliuma II, the last known Great King, comes to the throne
events.detail: Hattusili's son Tudhaliya IV lost ground to Assyria, which defeated him at Nihriya, though he briefly took Cyprus. Around 1207 BCE his younger son Suppiluliuma II succeeded his brother Arnuwanda III amid signs of disloyalty at court. He fought to restore control of southern Anatolia, crushing the rebel city of Tarhuntassa, and his fleet won the first recorded naval battle in history off Cyprus. But urgent grain shipments from Egypt point to famine, and enemies were advancing along the coasts from the west. He is the last Great King of Hatti known for certain.

events.text: Hattusa is gradually abandoned as the empire collapses
events.detail: Around 1190 BCE, as the Late Bronze Age collapse swept the eastern Mediterranean, the Hittite capital came to an end. Excavations suggest Hattusa was gradually abandoned over several decades, possibly amid regional drought; the court may have moved elsewhere, and fire destroyed what remained only after the elites had left. Suppiluliuma II's fate is unknown, and no Hittite king ever returned. The empire vanished as a state and disappears from the map. Only an offshoot survived at Carchemish, whose ruler Kuzi-Teshub, a descendant of Suppiluliuma I, later claimed the title 'Great King'.

events.text: Ugarit, a Hittite vassal on the Syrian coast, is destroyed
events.detail: Ugarit, a wealthy port on the Syrian coast, had been a Hittite vassal since the days of Suppiluliuma I, trading with Egypt, Cyprus and the Aegean and shipping grain around the region. Its last king, Ammurapi, sent his troops to help the Hittites and his ships to Lukka in Anatolia, leaving his own kingdom exposed. In a famous letter he described enemy ships arriving and his cities burned. Around 1185 BCE Ugarit was destroyed, one of many cities lost in the Late Bronze Age collapse, and with it the Hittites lost their last great ally on the Mediterranean coast.

name: Egypt's New Kingdom empire
summary: Ahmose I expelled the Hyksos and reunited Egypt (c. 1549–1524 BCE); his successors, above all Thutmose III, built an empire from Nubia beyond the Fourth Cataract to the Euphrates. Egypt contested Syria with Mitanni and then the Hittites until the treaty of c. 1259 BCE, but after Ramesses III fought off the Sea Peoples its power ebbed, and by Ramesses XI's death in 1077 BCE the country was split between Tanis and Thebes. Reign dates follow the conventional low chronology and are approximate.

events.text: Ahmose I becomes king at Thebes and continues the war on the Hyksos
events.detail: For about a century the Hyksos, kings of Near Eastern origin, had ruled northern Egypt from Avaris in the Delta, while a native dynasty held Thebes in the south. Ahmose's father, Seqenenre Tao, probably died fighting them, and his brother Kamose raided the lands around Avaris before dying after a short reign. Ahmose came to the throne as a boy of about ten, so the war paused under a regency. His reign, conventionally dated c. 1549–1524 BCE, would finish the struggle and is counted as the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty and the New Kingdom.

events.text: Ahmose takes Avaris, then Sharuhen after a 3-year siege: Egypt reunited
events.detail: Once grown, Ahmose moved down the eastern Delta and seized the border fortress of Tjaru, cutting Avaris off from help in Canaan. According to the tomb inscription of a soldier, Ahmose son of Ebana, the king attacked Avaris several times and took it on the fourth attempt, probably by his 18th or 19th regnal year. He then besieged the Hyksos stronghold of Sharuhen near Gaza for three years. With the Hyksos gone, Upper and Lower Egypt were one kingdom again, ruled from Thebes, and Egyptian armies stood on the edge of Canaan.

events.text: Thutmose I conquers Lower Nubia and reaches the Euphrates at Carchemish
events.detail: Thutmose I, a military man who came to power through marriage into the royal family, set out to push Egypt's borders further than ever. In Nubia he built a fortress at Tombos near the Third Cataract, and an inscription of his has been found at Kurgus, beyond the Fourth Cataract. In the Levant he marched to the Euphrates, becoming the first pharaoh to cross it, and set up a victory stele there. The Syrian princes stopped paying tribute after he left, but his campaigns marked out the frontiers, from Nubia to the Euphrates, that later kings tried to hold.

events.text: Child-king Thutmose III accedes; Hatshepsut rules, first as regent
events.detail: When Thutmose II died, his heir Thutmose III was a small child (estimates of his age range from two to 13). His stepmother and aunt Hatshepsut, Thutmose II's widow and a daughter of Thutmose I, acted as regent. By about the seventh year of the reign she had taken the full titles of a pharaoh and ruled as senior co-king, with Thutmose III as junior partner. Her roughly 20-year rule was mostly peaceful and prosperous, with major building at Karnak and trading expeditions. Thutmose III became sole ruler only at her death, c. 1458 BCE.

events.text: Thutmose III defeats a Canaanite coalition at Megiddo
events.detail: Soon after Hatshepsut died, the king of Kadesh led a coalition of Canaanite and Syrian rulers that gathered at Megiddo, a fortress controlling the main route north. Thutmose III marched from Egypt and, against his generals' advice, took his army through the narrow Aruna pass, surprising the enemy and routing them. The survivors fled into Megiddo, which surrendered after a siege of about seven months. The battle is usually dated 1457 BCE, though some place it in 1482 or 1479. Taking Megiddo gave Egypt control of northern Canaan and forced the Syrian princes to send tribute and hostages.

events.text: Thutmose III crosses the Euphrates to attack Mitanni
events.detail: Mitanni, a Hurrian kingdom in northern Syria and Mesopotamia, was Egypt's main rival for Syria. In his 33rd year (c. 1447 BCE), on his eighth campaign, Thutmose III had boats built at Byblos and carried them overland through Syria, past Aleppo and Carchemish. He crossed the Euphrates, catching the Mitannian king unprepared, pillaged towns on the far bank, and set up a stele beside the one left by his grandfather Thutmose I. The raid did not conquer Mitanni, but it showed Egypt's reach and brought gifts from distant kings, which Thutmose recorded as tribute.

events.text: Thutmose III campaigns in Nubia as far as the Fourth Cataract
events.detail: Egypt's southern empire in Nubia (Kush) supplied gold, ivory, ebony, cattle and soldiers, and was run by a viceroy. In his 50th year, about 1430 BCE, the aging Thutmose III led his last campaign, a march into Nubia as far as the Fourth Cataract of the Nile. No Egyptian king had taken an army so far south before, although Egyptian influence already reached the area around Gebel Barkal. By the end of his reign Egypt directly controlled the Nile valley up to the Fourth Cataract, its greatest southern extent.

events.text: Akhenaten promotes the Aten and moves the capital to Amarna
events.detail: Amenhotep IV came to the throne c. 1353 or 1351 BCE and in his fifth year renamed himself Akhenaten, 'beneficial to the Aten', the sun disc. He turned away from Amun and the traditional gods and founded a new capital, Akhetaten (modern Amarna), in Middle Egypt. The Amarna letters found there show his vassals in Syria and Canaan pleading for help as the Hittites under Suppiluliuma I replaced Mitanni as the great northern power. Egypt lost the province of Amurru when its ruler went over to the Hittites. After Akhenaten's death the old religion returned and Amarna was abandoned.

events.text: Ramesses I founds the 19th Dynasty
events.detail: Horemheb, a general who became the last king of the Eighteenth Dynasty, had no surviving children. He chose as heir his vizier Paramessu, an army officer from a military family in the Delta, who had a son, Seti, and a grandson to secure the succession. Paramessu took the throne as Ramesses I. His reign lasted only a year or two (often dated 1292–1290 BCE, though 1295–1294 is also cited), but he founded the Nineteenth Dynasty, whose kings Seti I and Ramesses II set out to win back Egypt's lost lands in Syria.

events.text: Ramesses II fights the Hittites at Kadesh
events.detail: Seti I had briefly recaptured Kadesh and Amurru, but both seem to have slipped back under Hittite control. In his fifth year, generally dated May 1274 BCE, Ramesses II marched north to retake them and met the Hittite king Muwatalli II near Kadesh on the Orontes River. With perhaps 5,000 to 6,000 chariots in all, it may be the largest chariot battle ever fought. Ramesses was ambushed and surrounded, then rallied his troops and drove the Hittites back. The battle ended in stalemate, but Muwatalli kept Kadesh and pushed into Egyptian territory, leaving Egypt's Asian empire limited to Canaan.

events.text: Peace treaty with the Hittites settles the Syrian frontier
events.detail: After Kadesh the fighting dragged on for years, while Egypt worried about the Sea Peoples and the Hittites about rising Assyria. Around 1259 BCE (some accounts give 1258, Ramesses II's 21st year), Ramesses and the Hittite king Hattusili III agreed what is the oldest surviving peace treaty. Both sides promised not to invade each other, to hand back political refugees, and to help each other against enemies. The treaty fixed the Syrian frontier where it stood, with Egypt keeping Canaan and the Hittites holding Kadesh and Amurru, and it kept the peace until the Hittite Empire collapsed decades later.

events.text: Ramesses III defeats the Sea Peoples on land at Djahy and at sea in the Delta
events.detail: Around 1200 BCE the Late Bronze Age world was falling apart, and groups that scholars call the Sea Peoples, among them the Peleset (Philistines) and Shardana, attacked the eastern Mediterranean. In his eighth year Ramesses III met them twice: on land at Djahy, on Egypt's frontier in the Levant, and in the Nile Delta, where his fleet ambushed their ships while archers lined the banks. Egypt survived when the Hittite Empire and many other states did not. But the cost was high, and the Philistines settled in southern Canaan as Egypt's hold on Asia faded.

events.text: Ramesses XI dies; Smendes (Tanis) and Amun's priests (Thebes) divide Egypt
events.detail: In the 20th Dynasty Egypt was hit by poor Nile floods, famine, unrest and corruption, and the loss of its empire in Asia. Under Ramesses XI, royal power weakened so far that the High Priests of Amun at Thebes became the real rulers of Upper Egypt, while Smendes controlled the north. When Ramesses XI died in 1077 BCE, Smendes buried him and founded the 21st Dynasty at Tanis in the Delta. The New Kingdom was over: Egypt entered the Third Intermediate Period, divided between Tanis and Thebes, with its foreign empire gone.

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: From 911 BCE Assyrian kings reconquered northern Mesopotamia, and Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III made Assyria the dominant power of the Near East. After a long spell of weak kings, Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727 BCE) more than doubled the empire, and the Sargonid kings took Israel, Babylon and, in 671 BCE, Egypt. Within two decades of Ashurbanipal's death the Babylonians and Medes destroyed Assur (614), Nineveh (612) and the last Assyrian army at Harran (609).

events.text: Adad-nirari II becomes king and begins reconquering northern Mesopotamia
events.detail: In the late 11th century BCE Assyria had lost most of its earlier empire, and Aramean tribes had settled across northern Mesopotamia. Adad-nirari II, king from 911 BCE, continued a slow reconquest begun by his father. He defeated and deported Arameans after a battle where the Khabur meets the Euphrates in 910, subdued peoples in eastern Anatolia, twice beat the king of Babylonia and annexed land north of the Diyala River. His reign is counted as the start of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, as Assyria began to win back the lands it had once ruled.

events.text: Ashurnasirpal II makes Nimrud (Kalhu) his capital
events.detail: Ashurnasirpal II (883–859 BCE) made Assyria the leading power of the Near East again. His campaigns reached the Mediterranean, where Phoenician cities paid him tribute, and he was notorious for brutality towards rebels. In 879 BCE he made Kalhu (Nimrud), a ruined town on the Tigris, his capital instead of the old city of Assur, using thousands of workers and captives to build walls, temples and a great palace. An inscription claims 69,574 guests attended its inauguration feast. Kalhu stayed the imperial capital until 706 BCE, while Assur remained the religious centre.

events.text: Shalmaneser III fights a Levantine coalition at Qarqar
events.detail: Shalmaneser III continued his father's wars and pushed west into Syria. In 853 BCE (854 in some reckonings) he met a coalition of about a dozen rulers at Qarqar on the Orontes River, led by Hadadezer of Damascus and including Ahab of Israel. His own inscription lists tens of thousands of enemy troops and thousands of chariots; the battle also contains the first known mention of Arabs. Shalmaneser claimed a great victory, but it was probably indecisive: the coalition kings kept their thrones and he had to fight them again several times. Assyria could not yet take the Levant.

events.text: Tiglath-Pileser III seizes power after the 'age of the magnates'
events.detail: After Shalmaneser III died in 824 BCE, Assyria entered the 'age of the magnates', when powerful generals and officials held real power and the kings were weak. Rivals grew bolder: in 754 BCE Urartu, a kingdom to the north, defeated the Assyrian army at Arpad. In 746/745 a revolt broke out in Kalhu, and Tiglath-Pileser III, most likely a usurper from within the royal family, took the throne. He reformed the army and the provinces, deported conquered peoples on a huge scale, and more than doubled the empire's territory.

events.text: Tiglath-Pileser III takes Babylon
events.detail: Babylonia, south of Assyria, was home to old cities and to Chaldean tribes whose chiefs fought over its throne. In 731 BCE the Chaldean chief Nabu-mukin-zeri made himself king of Babylon, which Tiglath-Pileser saw as a threat. After several years of war he captured Babylon in 729 BCE and proclaimed himself king of both Assyria and Babylon. From then on Assyria tried to rule Babylonia directly or through chosen kings, adding the rich south to the empire but also taking on a land that rebelled again and again.

events.text: Samaria falls, ending the Kingdom of Israel; Sargon II takes the throne
events.detail: The Kingdom of Israel, with its capital at Samaria, had rebelled against Assyrian overlordship. After a siege of several years, the Assyrians took Samaria in the 720s, ended the kingdom, deported much of its population and made it the province of Samerina. Sargon II later claimed the conquest, but historians think his predecessor Shalmaneser V more likely took the city. In 722 BCE Sargon, probably Shalmaneser's brother, seized the throne, most likely in a palace coup. He founded the Sargonid dynasty, which would rule Assyria at its height.

events.text: Sargon II defeats Rusa I of Urartu near Lake Urmia and sacks Musasir
events.detail: Urartu, centred around Lake Van, was Assyria's great rival in the north. In 714 BCE Sargon II marched into the mountains by a long route to surprise King Rusa I, defeated the Urartian army after Rusa tried to drive him back, and on the way home plundered the holy city of Musasir, carrying off enormous spoils. Sargon treated it as one of the great events of his reign and had the sack carved on his palace walls. Urartu stayed powerful and Rusa retook Musasir, but there were no more direct clashes between the two for the rest of Sargon's reign.

events.text: Sennacherib becomes king and makes Nineveh the capital
events.detail: In 705 BCE Sargon II was killed fighting in Anatolia and his body was never recovered, which Assyrians took as a sign of divine anger. His son Sennacherib abandoned Sargon's new capital at Dur-Sharrukin and moved the court to Nineveh, where he had lived as crown prince. There he launched one of the most ambitious building projects of the ancient world, with huge walls, temples, gardens and his 'Palace without Rival'. Nineveh remained the capital until the empire's fall. Sargon's death also set off revolts, above all in Babylonia, that Sennacherib spent years putting down.

events.text: Sennacherib invades the Levant and besieges Jerusalem
events.detail: Encouraged by Egypt and by the Babylonian rebel Marduk-apla-iddina, vassals in the Levant, including Hezekiah of Judah, stopped paying tribute. In 701 BCE Sennacherib marched west, took Sidon and Ashkelon, defeated an Egyptian army and captured most towns of Judah, including Lachish after a famous siege shown on his palace reliefs. He trapped Hezekiah in Jerusalem but did not take the city. The Bible tells of an angel destroying the Assyrian army, but Assyrian records show Hezekiah submitting, paying heavy tribute and losing land to Assyria's neighbouring vassals. Assyrian control of the Levant was restored.

events.text: Sennacherib destroys Babylon
events.detail: Babylon rebelled against Sennacherib repeatedly, often with help from Elam. In 694 BCE the Elamites captured his son Ashur-nadin-shumi, whom he had made king of Babylon, and probably executed him. A new Babylonian king, Mushezib-Marduk, then fought Sennacherib at Halule in 691, a battle both sides claimed to have won. Sennacherib besieged Babylon for over fifteen months and in 689 BCE took it and destroyed it, seizing the property of its gods. The destruction shocked Babylonians, and Sennacherib's son Esarhaddon later rebuilt the city.

events.text: Esarhaddon conquers Egypt: the empire's greatest extent
events.detail: Egypt, ruled by Kushite pharaohs, had long encouraged rebels against Assyria. Esarhaddon's first invasion, in 673 BCE, seems to have failed badly. In early 671 he marched again with a larger army, won three battles and captured and plundered Memphis, Egypt's capital. The conquest made the Assyrian Empire the largest the world had yet seen, reaching from the Nile across the Levant and Mesopotamia to the Zagros. It was hard to hold: Egypt rebelled repeatedly, and Psamtik I, at first an Assyrian vassal, had made it fully independent by 656 BCE.

events.text: Babylon falls to Ashurbanipal after his brother's revolt (652–648)
events.detail: Esarhaddon arranged that his son Ashurbanipal would rule the empire, while another son, Shamash-shum-ukin, would be king of Babylon. Resenting his younger brother's control, Shamash-shum-ukin revolted in 652 BCE and gathered a coalition of Assyria's enemies against him. Ashurbanipal besieged Babylon for two years; according to his account, the starving citizens even ate their own children. Babylon fell in 648 BCE, Shamash-shum-ukin died during the siege, and the city was plundered. Assyria kept Babylonia, but the war left it bitter towards Assyrian rule.

events.text: Ashurbanipal's army destroys Elam's centres and plunders Susa
events.detail: Elam, in south-western Iran, was Assyria's oldest enemy and had backed Babylonian rebels for decades. After earlier wars, Ashurbanipal's armies returned in 646 BCE, chased the Elamite king Humban-haltash into the mountains and crushed all of Elam's main centres. On the way home they plundered the ancient capital, Susa: according to Ashurbanipal's inscriptions they desecrated the royal tombs, looted the temples, carried off the statues of the gods and sowed salt in the ground. Elam's power was broken, and nearby peoples, including the Persians, began paying tribute to Assyria instead.

events.text: Medes and Babylonians sack Nineveh
events.detail: After Ashurbanipal died, around 631 BCE, Assyria was weakened by succession struggles, and Nabopolassar made Babylonia independent. The Medes under Cyaxares joined the war, sacking Assur in 614 BCE. In 612 the Medes and Babylonians besieged Nineveh, one of the greatest cities in the world, for about three months, then broke in, plundered and burned it. King Sin-shar-ishkun is assumed to have died in the sack. Assyria's heartland was lost, and only a remnant of the army escaped west under a new king, Ashur-uballit II.

events.text: Ashur-uballit II defeated at Harran: the empire ends
events.detail: Ashur-uballit II set himself up at Harran, in the west of the old empire, where he was backed by Egypt, which feared Babylonian power. Because Assur had fallen, he could not be crowned in the traditional way. In late 610 or early 609 BCE the Babylonians and Medes captured Harran, and a few months later an attempt by Ashur-uballit and an Egyptian army to retake it failed disastrously. Ashur-uballit then disappears from the records. The Neo-Assyrian Empire was gone, and its lands were divided between the Babylonians in the west and south and the Medes in the north and east.

reigns.name: Age of the magnates (Shamshi-Adad V to Ashur-nirari V)

name: Neo-Babylonian Empire (Nebuchadnezzar II)
summary: Nabopolassar threw off Assyrian rule in 626 BCE and, allied with the Medes, destroyed Assyria by 609 BCE. His son Nebuchadnezzar II (605–562 BCE) won Syria and the Levant at Carchemish, destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BCE and rebuilt Babylon in splendour. After his death three short reigns ended in Nabonidus, whose long absence in Arabia left Babylon exposed; Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BCE.

events.text: Nabopolassar seizes Babylon and Nippur and is crowned king
events.detail: Babylonia had been ruled by Assyria for more than a century, and a civil war in Assyria after Ashurbanipal's death left the south unstable. Nabopolassar, a man of unclear origin who called himself 'son of a nobody', seized Babylon and Nippur in 626 BCE. The Assyrians struck back, retaking Nippur and besieging him at Uruk and in Babylon, but both sieges failed. On 22/23 November 626 BCE he was crowned king of Babylon. Babylonia was independent again, though it took nearly ten more years of fighting to push the Assyrians out completely.

events.text: Medes take Assur; Nabopolassar allies with them
events.detail: By 616 BCE Nabopolassar was carrying the war into Assyria itself, but he could not break it alone. In 615 or 614 the Medes of western Iran under King Cyaxares invaded Assyria. In the summer of 614 BCE they besieged Assur, the ancient religious heart of Assyria, and sacked it brutally; even the hostile Babylonian chronicles were shocked. Nabopolassar arrived after the sack, met Cyaxares and signed an alliance against Assyria, sealed by the marriage of his son Nebuchadnezzar to Cyaxares's daughter Amytis. Together the two powers now had the strength to destroy the Assyrian Empire.

events.text: Nineveh falls after a siege
events.detail: In 612 BCE the Babylonians and Medes joined forces against Nineveh, Assyria's capital and one of the largest cities in the world. After a siege of about three months, they broke through in August and plundered and burned the city, massacring many of its people. The Assyrian king Sin-shar-ishkun probably died defending it, and other Assyrian cities such as Nimrud were also attacked. The Assyrian heartland was lost; a remnant of the army fled west to Harran. Babylon now stood to inherit Assyria's lands in Mesopotamia, Syria and the Levant.

events.text: Last Assyrian king defeated at Harran
events.detail: The last Assyrian ruler, Ashur-uballit II, held out at Harran in the west, backed by Egypt, which wanted Assyria to survive as a buffer against Babylon and the Medes. In late 610 or early 609 BCE the Babylonians and Medes took Harran. A few months later Ashur-uballit and an Egyptian army under Pharaoh Necho II tried to retake the city and failed, and Ashur-uballit disappears from history. Assyria was finished, but Egypt kept fighting, and Necho's army held Syria and the Levant as far as Carchemish on the Euphrates.

events.text: Crown prince Nebuchadnezzar routs Egypt at Carchemish, then becomes king
events.detail: Necho II had made Carchemish, a key crossing and trading city on the Euphrates, his base in Syria. Around 605 BCE, Nabopolassar, perhaps ill, sent his eldest son and crown prince Nebuchadnezzar in sole command. Nebuchadnezzar crossed the river, crushed the Egyptian army and chased the survivors to the region of Hamath. News then came that Nabopolassar had died, and Nebuchadnezzar hurried back to Babylon, where he was proclaimed king in mid-August. The victory opened Syria and the Levant to Babylon and made it the dominant power of the Near East.

events.text: Nebuchadnezzar II destroys Ashkelon
events.detail: After Carchemish, Nebuchadnezzar marched west almost every year to make the cities of the Levant accept his rule; the rulers of Phoenicia swore loyalty to him. In 604 BCE he attacked Ashkelon (Ascalon), a Philistine port on the coast, which had looked to Egypt for support. According to the Babylonian Chronicle its king was captured and taken to Babylon, and the city was plundered and levelled; excavations at the site confirm that it was largely destroyed then. The harsh example warned other cities in the region what rebellion would cost.

events.text: Invasion of Egypt ends in heavy losses on both sides
events.detail: Even after its defeat at Carchemish, Egypt kept great influence in the Levant and encouraged cities there to resist Babylon. In 601 BCE Nebuchadnezzar took the risky step of marching across the Sinai to invade Egypt itself. According to the Babylonian Chronicle, both armies suffered huge numbers of casualties, and the invasion failed. Nebuchadnezzar spent the next year in Babylon rebuilding his chariot forces. Egypt was not conquered, and the setback may have encouraged Judah and others to rebel, though Necho II gave up his own ambitions in the Levant.

events.text: Jerusalem taken; King Jehoiachin deported to Babylon
events.detail: Jehoiakim, king of Judah, stopped obeying Babylon around 601 BCE, expecting help from Egypt. Nebuchadnezzar marched on Jerusalem in late 598 BCE, and the Babylonian Chronicle records that he took the city on 2 Addaru (March) 597 BCE and captured its king. Jehoiakim had died during the siege, and his young son Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) was taken to Babylon, where later records list him receiving food rations at the palace. Nebuchadnezzar installed Jehoiachin's uncle Zedekiah as king and carried off heavy tribute, keeping Judah as a vassal state.

events.text: Jerusalem destroyed after Zedekiah's revolt; Babylonian captivity begins
events.detail: Encouraged by Egypt, Zedekiah refused tribute to Babylon in 589 BCE. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, according to the Bible for 18 to 30 months, and in the summer of 587 BCE (some date it 586) took and destroyed the city and its temple. Zedekiah was captured, his sons were executed, and he was blinded and taken to Babylon. Much of the population was deported to Babylonia, beginning the Babylonian captivity, and archaeology confirms Jerusalem was destroyed and emptied. The Kingdom of Judah ended, and the southern Levant became a Babylonian province.

events.text: Tyre submits after a siege begun c. 586
events.detail: Tyre, a rich Phoenician port, had rebelled around the same time as Judah. Part of the city stood on an island about 800 metres off the coast and could not be taken without a navy. Nebuchadnezzar's siege is said to have lasted 13 years, usually dated c. 586 to 573 BCE, though the length comes only from the historian Josephus and is debated. The Babylonians destroyed the mainland town but never took the island. In the end the Tyrians negotiated a surrender, and Tyre remained under its own vassal kings, more tightly controlled by Babylon.

events.text: Nebuchadnezzar II dies in Babylon
events.detail: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled for 43 years, the longest of the Neo-Babylonian kings, and is remembered as the empire's greatest. Besides his wars, he rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale: the temple of Marduk (Esagila), the great ziggurat Etemenanki, palaces, the processional way and the Ishtar Gate. His later attacks on Egypt failed, and his empire's borders grew little after Carchemish. He died in Babylon in 562 BCE. His son Amel-Marduk followed, but was soon overthrown, the first of three short reigns that weakened the dynasty.

events.text: Nabonidus takes the throne after Labashi-Marduk is assassinated
events.detail: Neriglissar, who had seized the throne from Amel-Marduk, died in 556 BCE, and his son Labashi-Marduk became king. Within one to three months he was deposed and murdered in a plot probably led by Belshazzar, son of an elderly official named Nabonidus, who was then proclaimed king. Nabonidus was not of Babylonian royal descent; his mother came from Harran in former Assyria and was devoted to the moon god Sin. His favour for Sin over Babylon's great god Marduk soon set him at odds with Babylon's priests and leaders.

events.text: Nabonidus returns from about ten years at Tayma in Arabia
events.detail: In 553 BCE Nabonidus left Babylon on campaign in Arabia and then stayed at the oasis of Tayma in northern Arabia from 552 to 543/542 BCE. Why he went is unknown, but quarrels with Babylon's priests and elite may be the reason. His son Belshazzar ruled Babylonia as regent, while Nabonidus remained king. Babylon's great New Year festival was suspended while he was away. When Nabonidus returned, he pushed his favour for Sin harder, rebuilding Sin's temple at Harran, deepening the anger of the Marduk priesthood as Persia grew stronger on Babylon's borders.

events.text: Cyrus wins at Opis; his army enters Babylon on 12 October
events.detail: By 539 BCE Babylonia was the last great power in western Asia outside Persian control. In September or October of that year, Cyrus the Great invaded and defeated the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris, north of Babylon. Sippar then surrendered, and on 12 October Persian forces entered Babylon. Babylonian sources say they took it without a battle, while Greek historians describe a siege. Nabonidus was captured but, according to several sources, spared, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, the last kingdom ruled by native Mesopotamian kings, passed to Persia.

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes in 550 BCE and took Lydia and Babylon; Cambyses added Egypt and Darius I pushed the frontier to the Indus and into Europe, ruling c. 5.5 million km², the largest empire yet seen. Defeats in Greece (490, 480–479 BCE) and the loss of Egypt (404–343 BCE) dented but did not break it; Alexander of Macedon destroyed it in 334–330 BCE.

events.text: Cyrus defeats the Medes and takes Ecbatana
events.detail: Cyrus, king of the small Persian realm of Anshan in south-western Iran from 559 BCE, was a vassal of his grandfather Astyages, king of the Medes, whose empire stretched across much of Iran and beyond. According to the Nabonidus Chronicle, Astyages attacked Cyrus, but part of the Median army mutinied; Herodotus says the general Harpagus defected to Cyrus. After fighting that lasted about three years (553–550 BCE), Cyrus captured Astyages and took the Median capital Ecbatana. The Median Empire's lands and vassals passed to Cyrus, turning Persia almost overnight into the leading power of Iran.

events.text: Cyrus conquers Lydia and captures Sardis
events.detail: Croesus, the rich king of Lydia in western Anatolia, attacked Persian territory in Cappadocia and took the city of Pteria. Cyrus marched west; after an indecisive battle at Pteria, Croesus fell back to his capital, Sardis, expecting to wait for allies. Cyrus instead followed him in winter, routed the Lydian cavalry (Herodotus says the horses panicked at the smell of his camels) and captured Sardis and Croesus. The date is uncertain: 547 BCE was long accepted, but 546 is also given. Lydia and soon the Greek cities of Ionia came under Persian rule, carrying the empire to the Aegean.

events.text: Cyrus takes Babylon and its empire
events.detail: Babylonia was the last great power in western Asia outside Persian rule, and its king Nabonidus was unpopular with Babylon's priests. In 539 BCE Cyrus defeated the Babylonian army at Opis on the Tigris, Sippar surrendered, and his forces entered Babylon in October, by Babylonian accounts without a battle. On the Cyrus Cylinder he presented himself as chosen by Babylon's god Marduk and claimed to have returned displaced peoples and restored temples; the Bible records his decree letting the Jewish exiles return to Jerusalem. Babylon's empire, probably including Syria and the Levant, became Persian.

events.text: Cambyses II defeats Psamtik III at Pelusium and conquers Egypt
events.detail: Egypt, under the Twenty-sixth Dynasty, was the last great independent kingdom of the Near East. Cyrus's son Cambyses II built a navy from Phoenician and Anatolian ships and made a treaty with the Arabs who controlled the desert route. In spring 525 BCE he defeated the new pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium on Egypt's eastern border; one later story says he put animals sacred to the Egyptians in his front line. He then besieged and took Memphis. By summer all Egypt was under Persian rule, and the Libyans and the Greeks of Cyrene soon submitted too.

events.text: Darius I seizes the throne after the disputed succession
events.detail: In 522 BCE Cambyses died on his way back from Egypt to deal with a revolt by a man claiming to be his brother Bardiya. According to Darius's own Behistun Inscription, the real Bardiya had been secretly killed, and the rebel was an impostor named Gaumata. In September 522 Darius, a distant relative of Cyrus, and six other nobles killed the man at the fortress of Sikayauvati. Most modern historians doubt this story and suspect Darius invented it to justify seizing the throne. Darius then faced revolts across the empire and crushed them all, then reorganised the empire into satrapies with a common coinage.

events.text: Darius conquers the lands around the Indus (Hindush)
events.detail: Cyrus may already have taken Gandhara in the far east of the empire, and Darius's Behistun Inscription lists it as Persian by about 518 BCE. According to one reconstruction, in 516 BCE Darius campaigned through Central Asia and Afghanistan to Taxila, wintered in Gandhara, and in 515 conquered the lands around the Indus River. His inscriptions list a new province, Hindush, whose exact location is uncertain, and according to Herodotus he sent the Greek Scylax of Caryanda to sail down the Indus and back to Egypt. The Indus valley became the empire's eastern frontier and, according to Herodotus, a rich source of gold.

events.text: Darius invades European Scythia and subdues parts of the Balkans
events.detail: The Scythians were nomads living north of the Black Sea and Danube who threatened Persia's northern borders and trade. Around 513 BCE Darius crossed the Bosporus on a bridge of boats, marched through Thrace and crossed the Danube into Scythia. The Scythians refused battle, retreating and laying waste the land, and after a month of chasing them Darius's army, worn down by hunger and sickness, turned back. The campaign itself won no territory beyond the Danube, but it brought Thrace under Persian rule and made Macedonia a vassal, extending the empire into Europe.

events.text: Ionian Revolt begins, the first great war between Greeks and Persia
events.detail: Persia ruled the Greek cities of Ionia, on Anatolia's west coast, through local tyrants. In 499 BCE Aristagoras, tyrant of Miletus, led a failed Persian expedition against Naxos and, fearing he would lose his power, stirred Ionia to revolt. With help from Athens and Eretria, the rebels burned Sardis in 498, and the revolt spread to Caria and Cyprus. Persia struck back, crushed the Ionian fleet at Lade in 494 and took Miletus, and by 493 the revolt was over. Darius then set out to punish Athens and Eretria, starting the Greco-Persian Wars.

events.text: Persian expedition defeated at Marathon
events.detail: To punish Athens and Eretria for helping the Ionian Revolt, Darius sent a fleet under Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean in 490 BCE. After subduing the Cyclades and sacking Eretria, the Persians landed at Marathon, near Athens. The Athenians, helped by Plataea and led by the general Miltiades, attacked and enveloped the Persian centre with their strengthened flanks. According to Herodotus, 6,400 Persians died against 192 Athenians. The Persians sailed back to Asia, and Darius began raising a new army, but a revolt in Egypt in 486 and his death delayed the next invasion.

events.text: Xerxes invades Greece; his fleet is beaten at Salamis
events.detail: Darius's son Xerxes led a vast invasion of Greece by land and sea in 480 BCE. After the Spartan-led rearguard was destroyed at Thermopylae, the Persians took and burned Athens, whose people had been evacuated. The Athenian general Themistocles lured the larger Persian fleet into the narrow straits off the island of Salamis, where it was badly beaten. Xerxes returned to Asia with much of his army, and in 479 the force he left behind was defeated at Plataea and the fleet at Mycale. Persia never again tried to conquer mainland Greece.

events.text: Egypt breaks away under Amyrtaeus
events.detail: Egypt had rebelled against Persian rule several times. Amyrtaeus, probably a relative of the old Saite kings, had led a guerrilla war in the western Delta since about 411 BCE. When Darius II died in 404, the new king Artaxerxes II gathered an army to retake Egypt, but a struggle with his brother Cyrus the Younger kept it from marching. Amyrtaeus became pharaoh in 404, though Persian rule was still recognised in the far south until about 401. Egypt, one of the empire's richest provinces, stayed independent for roughly six decades.

events.text: Artaxerxes III reconquers Egypt
events.detail: Artaxerxes III, who killed many of his own relatives to secure his throne, was determined to win Egypt back. His first invasion, around 351 BCE, was crushed by Pharaoh Nectanebo II, and revolts followed in Phoenicia and Cyprus. After crushing those, he led a huge army with Greek mercenaries into Egypt, forced Pelusium and Bubastis to surrender, and drove Nectanebo to flee. The reconquest is traditionally dated 343 BCE, though many scholars now place it in 340 or 339. Egypt was harshly treated, its temples looted, and it stayed Persian until Alexander arrived.

events.text: Alexander invades and wins at the Granicus
events.detail: Philip II of Macedon had planned to invade Persia, and after his murder in 336 BCE his son Alexander took over the plan. In 334 Alexander crossed the Hellespont with an army of around 48,000 soldiers. In May he met the army of the Persian satraps of Asia Minor at the Granicus River and won, nearly losing his life in the cavalry fighting, then destroyed the Greek mercenaries in Persian service. Sardis surrendered with its treasury, and the Greek cities of the coast followed. Western Anatolia was lost to Persia.

events.text: Alexander defeats Darius III at Gaugamela
events.detail: After defeating Darius III at Issus in 333 BCE, Alexander took the Levant and Egypt, then marched into Mesopotamia. Darius gathered a huge army and met him at Gaugamela, north of Arbela (modern Erbil), on 1 October 331 BCE. Though heavily outnumbered, the Macedonians won through better tactics, and Darius fled east. Babylon surrendered to Alexander, followed by Susa and the Persian capital Persepolis, with their vast treasuries. Darius would never raise another imperial army, and the empire's western and central heartlands now belonged to Alexander.

events.text: Darius III is killed; the empire passes to Alexander
events.detail: After Gaugamela, Darius III fled to Ecbatana and then east towards Bactria, hoping to raise another army, while Alexander burned Persepolis and pursued him. In 330 BCE, as Alexander closed in, Darius was murdered by his relative Bessus, satrap of Bactria, and other nobles. Alexander gave him a royal burial at Persepolis, then hunted down Bessus, who had claimed the throne, and had him executed. Most remaining satraps went over to Alexander. The Achaemenid Empire, which had lasted some 220 years, ended, and its lands became part of Alexander's empire.
