name: Roman Republic and Empire
summary: The Roman Republic (from c. 509 BCE) conquered Italy, then defeated Carthage and the Hellenistic kingdoms to dominate the Mediterranean, before civil wars ended in one-man rule under Augustus (27 BCE). The Empire peaked under Trajan at about 5 million km² (117 CE), survived the crisis of the third century, and was split for good between East and West in 395. The Western half lost its provinces to Germanic peoples and ended when Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in 476.

events.text: Monarchy overthrown; the Republic, led by two annual consuls, begins
events.detail: According to Roman tradition, Rome was ruled by kings until the last of them, Tarquinius Superbus, was driven out after his son Sextus raped the noblewoman Lucretia. The rebels replaced the monarchy with a republic in which two consuls, elected every year, held the highest power, so that no single man could rule for life. The traditional date of 509 BCE comes from a chronology assembled centuries later, and many modern scholars treat the story as largely legendary. Whatever the details, the new Republic was still only a small city-state on the Tiber, one power among many in central Italy.

events.text: Rome defeats the Latin League and dominates Latium
events.detail: In the 4th century BCE Rome led a league of neighbouring Latin cities, but the Latins resented its growing dominance and went to war in 340 BCE. After defeats at Trifanum and finally at Pedum in 338 BCE, the Latin League was dissolved. Rome did not simply crush the Latins: their territory was brought into the Roman sphere, and the cities received partial rights or varying levels of Roman citizenship that tied them to Rome. The settlement made Rome master of Latium and gave it a model for ruling conquered Italians that fuelled its expansion across the peninsula.

events.text: Tarentum surrenders: Rome controls peninsular Italy
events.detail: The Greek city of Tarentum in southern Italy feared Roman expansion, and in 281 BCE it invited King Pyrrhus of Epirus to fight on its side. Pyrrhus beat the Romans at Heraclea and Asculum, but at such cost that a 'Pyrrhic victory' became a byword, and after fighting at Beneventum in 275 BCE he withdrew to Greece. In 272 BCE Tarentum fell to Rome, and its Epirote garrison was allowed to sail home. Rome now controlled peninsular Italy, and its victory over a Hellenistic king showed that it had become a major Mediterranean power.

events.text: First Punic War won; Sicily becomes the first province
events.detail: Rome's first war with Carthage, the great sea power of North Africa, began in 264 BCE over Messana in Sicily and lasted 23 years, the greatest naval war of antiquity. After immense losses on both sides, the Romans slowly occupied most of the island. In 241 BCE a Roman fleet destroyed a Carthaginian relief force off the Aegates Islands, leaving Carthage's army in Sicily cut off and forcing it to seek peace. Carthage paid large reparations and gave up Sicily, which became Rome's first province outside Italy and the start of an overseas empire.

events.text: Rome defeats Carthage at Zama, winning the Second Punic War
events.detail: In the Second Punic War Hannibal invaded Italy, but Rome fought back in Spain, where Scipio cleared out the Carthaginians in five years, and then carried the war to Africa. Carthage recalled Hannibal from Italy to defend the homeland. At Zama in 202 BCE, in what is now Tunisia, Scipio's army of about 40,000, stronger in cavalry, defeated Hannibal's larger force and its 80 war elephants. The peace stripped Carthage of all its lands outside Africa and some within it. Spain passed to Rome, and Carthage was left a subordinate power, no longer a rival for the western Mediterranean.

events.text: Carthage destroyed; Achaean League crushed at Corinth
events.detail: By the mid-2nd century BCE Rome dominated the Mediterranean but still crushed any sign of resistance. In the Third Punic War (149–146 BCE) a Roman army besieged Carthage; in 146 the city was stormed and systematically destroyed, and some 50,000 survivors were sold into slavery. The same year, in Greece, the consul Lucius Mummius defeated the Achaean League at Corinth, burned the city and enslaved its women and children. Carthage's lands became the Roman province of Africa, and the rest of Greece fell under Roman control beside the new province of Macedonia.

events.text: Caesar's Gallic Wars begin with the campaign against the Helvetii
events.detail: Julius Caesar, an ambitious general deep in debt, wanted military glory to boost his political career. In 58 BCE the migration of the Helvetii from what is now Switzerland gave him a reason to intervene in Gaul, and by 57 he had resolved to conquer all of it. Over the following years he fought Gallic, Germanic and British peoples, crossing twice to Britain, and in 52 BCE he crushed the great revolt led by Vercingetorix at the siege of Alesia. Rome's rule now extended over the whole of Gaul (present-day France, Belgium and Switzerland), pushing its frontier to the Rhine.

events.text: Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra at Actium; Egypt annexed in 30
events.detail: After Julius Caesar's murder, his heir Octavian and the general Mark Antony shared power, but Antony allied himself with Cleopatra VII of Egypt and the two men became rivals. On 2 September 31 BCE Octavian's fleet, commanded by Marcus Agrippa, defeated Antony and Cleopatra off Actium in western Greece. Octavian pursued them to Alexandria, which fell on 1 August 30 BCE, and both took their own lives. Egypt, the last surviving kingdom of Alexander's successors, was annexed, and Octavian, given the name Augustus in 27 BCE, ruled as the first emperor: the Republic had given way to one-man rule.

events.text: Germanic coalition destroys three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest
events.detail: Under Augustus, Rome tried to bring Germania, the lands beyond the Rhine, under its control. In 9 CE the governor Publius Quinctilius Varus led three legions and their auxiliaries into the Teutoburg Forest, where they were ambushed and destroyed by a Germanic alliance led by Arminius, a chieftain who had served as an officer in Varus's own auxiliary troops. Later campaigns under Tiberius and Germanicus took revenge but did not reconquer the region. The disaster ended Augustus's expansion in the north, and the Rhine became the lasting border between the Empire and free Germania.

events.text: Trajan dies with the empire at its greatest extent
events.detail: Trajan, emperor from 98 to 117 CE, was a soldier-emperor who led one of Rome's greatest military expansions. He conquered Dacia north of the Danube and annexed Nabataea in Arabia, then attacked the Parthian Empire and made Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria into provinces. In August 117 he fell ill while sailing back to Rome and died at Selinus in Asia Minor, with the empire at its largest, about 5 million km². His successor Hadrian quickly abandoned Mesopotamia as too costly and distant to defend, so the eastern frontier pulled back again.

events.text: Valerian captured by Persia; the Gallic Empire breaks away
events.detail: The third century brought civil wars, invasions and economic trouble. Emperor Valerian left the West to his son Gallienus and marched east against the Sasanian Persians, but after the Battle of Edessa in 260 CE he was captured by Shapur I, the first Roman emperor ever taken prisoner in battle. With much of the eastern army lost, Postumus, the commander on the Rhine, declared himself emperor and founded the breakaway Gallic Empire, which at its height held Gaul, Britain, Hispania and the Germanies. By 268 the empire had split into three states, until Aurelian reunited it by 274.

events.text: Theodosius I dies; the empire is split between Arcadius and Honorius
events.detail: Theodosius I, emperor from 379, won two civil wars and became the last emperor to rule the whole Roman world. He had already made his two young sons co-emperors, and when he died in January 395 they succeeded him jointly: Arcadius in the East, ruling from Constantinople, and Honorius, aged ten, in the West. The split followed a long practice of shared rule, but this time it proved permanent. From now on the map shows two separate empires: the Eastern half would survive for another thousand years, while the West entered its final decline.

events.text: Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome; Britain effectively abandoned
events.detail: After years of failed bargaining with the Western court at Ravenna over land and rank for his people, the Visigothic king Alaric besieged Rome and starved it into submission. On 24 August 410 his men entered the city and plundered it for three days, the first time in almost 800 years that Rome had fallen to a foreign enemy. The same year Honorius refused Britain's appeal for military help: the last mobile troops had left the island with the usurper Constantine III in 407, and the Romano-British had expelled Roman officials. Britain slipped out of the Empire for good.

events.text: Vandals take Carthage and the rich African provinces
events.detail: The Vandals, a Germanic people, crossed from Spain to North Africa in 429 under their king Gaiseric (Geiseric) and conquered much of the coast of today's Algeria and Tunisia. In 439 Gaiseric broke a treaty with Rome and took Carthage, apparently without a fight while many of its people were at the races. North Africa had been a major source of tax revenue and of the grain that fed Rome, so its loss crippled the Western Empire. The Vandals went on to seize Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica, and sacked Rome itself in 455.

events.text: Odoacer deposes Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna: end of the Western Empire
events.detail: By the 470s the Western emperors were puppets of powerful generals and controlled little beyond Italy. In 475 the general Orestes drove out Julius Nepos and put his young son Romulus on the throne. When Orestes refused to give Italian land to the barbarian troops in Roman service, they rallied behind their officer Odoacer, who killed Orestes and took Ravenna on 4 September 476, deposing Romulus. Odoacer named no new emperor, ruled as king of Italy, and the imperial insignia were sent to the Eastern emperor Zeno: the Western Roman Empire was gone from the map.

name: Empire of Alexander the Great
summary: Philip II (359–336 BCE) made Macedon the master of Greece; his son Alexander III conquered the whole Persian Empire and pushed on to the Indus before dying in Babylon in 323 BCE. His generals kept the empire nominally united under his half-brother and infant son, but after both were murdered they took royal titles, and the battle of Ipsus (301 BCE) fixed its partition into rival kingdoms.

events.text: Philip II becomes king of Macedon and reforms its army
events.detail: Macedon, in northern Greece, was a weak kingdom on the edge of Greek affairs when King Perdiccas III was killed fighting the Illyrians in 359 BCE. His brother Philip, who had spent years as a hostage in Thebes learning from its general Epaminondas, was named regent for Perdiccas's infant son but soon took the throne himself. He rebuilt the army around the Macedonian phalanx, combined it with cavalry, and made skilled use of siege engines, diplomacy and marriage alliances. In less than 25 years this reformed army turned Macedon into the dominant power in Greece.

events.text: Philip takes Amphipolis, opening Macedon's eastward expansion
events.detail: Amphipolis, a city in Thrace, commanded the gold mines of Mount Pangaion, and Athens had long tried and failed to recover it. In 357 BCE Philip besieged and took the city after agreeing to hand it over to Athens in exchange for Pydna; instead he captured Pydna too and kept both, and Athens declared war. In 356 he also seized nearby Crenides, renamed it Philippi and garrisoned its mines. The gold from this region paid for much of Philip's later campaigning, and Macedon's power now reached east along the northern Aegean coast.

events.text: Philip defeats Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea
events.detail: Philip's growing power alarmed the Greek city-states, and Athens and Thebes led an alliance against him. In August 338 BCE the armies met at Chaeronea in Boeotia; Philip, with roughly 30,000 infantry and 2,000 cavalry according to Diodorus, commanded the right wing, while his 18-year-old son Alexander led the left. The Macedonian victory was decisive. Philip then created the League of Corinth, which bound the Greek states to Macedon as allies, and was chosen to lead a pan-Hellenic war against Persia. Mainland Greece was now under Macedonian leadership.

events.text: Philip assassinated at Aegae; Alexander III becomes king
events.detail: In October 336 BCE Philip's court gathered at Aegae, the old Macedonian capital, for the wedding of his daughter Cleopatra to King Alexander of Epirus. As Philip entered the theatre, unguarded so as to appear approachable to Greek visitors, he was stabbed to death by Pausanias of Orestis, one of his own bodyguards. His 20-year-old son Alexander took the throne at once. Alexander inherited not just Macedon and its control of Greece but also his father's army and his planned invasion of the Persian Empire, whose advance guard was already in Asia Minor.

events.text: Alexander crosses into Asia; victory at the Granicus
events.detail: In 334 BCE Alexander crossed the Hellespont into Asia with the army of Macedon and its Greek allies, beginning his war on the Persian Empire. In May the Persian satraps (governors) of Asia Minor, with Greek mercenaries under Memnon of Rhodes, tried to stop him at the crossing of the Granicus river, the modern Biga in Turkey. Alexander forced the crossing and destroyed their army; the captured Greek mercenaries were sent to Macedon as slaves. Sardis and Ephesus soon fell, and the Persians were left defending isolated cities in Asia Minor.

events.text: Alexander defeats Darius III at Issus
events.detail: After the Granicus, King Darius III took personal command of a huge Persian army and advanced into Syria to stop Alexander. On 5 November 333 BCE the armies met at Issus in southern Anatolia, where Darius had to fight on a narrow battlefield that favoured Alexander's smaller force. Alexander's attack broke the Persian line and Darius fled, leaving behind his treasury, his mother, his wife and his daughters, who were all captured. The victory gave Alexander complete control of southern Asia Minor and opened the road south into Syria and Phoenicia.

events.text: Alexandria founded in Egypt; Darius beaten again at Gaugamela
events.detail: After taking Tyre and Gaza in 332 BCE, Alexander entered Egypt, where he was welcomed as a liberator from Persian rule. During a few months there he reorganised its taxes and founded Alexandria, later the capital of the Ptolemaic kingdom and a great centre of Greek culture. In 331 he marched north-east to the Tigris and, at Gaugamela near Arbela (modern Erbil), heavily outnumbered, defeated Darius again with superior tactics. Darius fled to Ecbatana, and Alexander took Babylon, Susa and Persepolis with their treasuries: the Persian heartland was now his.

events.text: Darius III is killed by Bessus; the Persian Empire is Alexander's
events.detail: After Gaugamela, Darius III fled east, but his authority was collapsing. In 330 BCE, as Alexander closed in, Darius was taken prisoner by Bessus, satrap of Bactria and his own kinsman, whose men stabbed the Great King to death; Bessus then proclaimed himself king as Artaxerxes V. Alexander gave Darius a royal burial and presented himself as his avenger and the rightful heir of the Achaemenids. The Persian Empire was now Alexander's, though he spent the next years fighting Bessus and rebels in Bactria and Sogdiana, founding cities such as Alexandria Eschate in modern Tajikistan.

events.text: Alexander defeats Porus at the Hydaspes; his army mutinies at the Beas
events.detail: After conquering Persia, Alexander crossed into the Punjab, where King Porus of the Paurava kingdom blocked the Hydaspes (Jhelum) river with an army that included war elephants. In May 326 BCE Alexander crossed the monsoon-swollen river away from Porus's camp to catch him in the flank, and defeated him in what was possibly his costliest battle; he then made Porus a satrap, effectively restoring him as ruler. Pushing east, his exhausted army refused to go beyond the Hyphasis (Beas) river. The mutiny ended the expedition: Alexander turned back, and the Beas became the eastern limit of his empire.

events.text: Alexander reaches Susa after a costly march through the desert
events.detail: On the way back from India, Alexander split his forces. Craterus led part of the army through Carmania, the admiral Nearchus explored the coast of the Persian Gulf by sea, and Alexander took the rest on the harder southern route through the Gedrosian Desert and Makran. Many men died in the desert before he reached Susa in 324 BCE, where he executed several satraps and governors who had misbehaved in his absence. Back in the heart of the empire, he tried to bind Persians and Macedonians together, and his veterans mutinied at Opis over his adoption of Persian customs.

events.text: Alexander dies in Babylon; Perdiccas becomes regent of the empire
events.detail: Alexander returned to Babylon, which he had planned to make the capital of his empire, and was preparing an invasion of Arabia when he died there on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE, aged 32. He left no adult heir, and his officers argued over the succession. In the settlement known as the Partition of Babylon, his half-brother Arrhidaeus (as Philip III) and the child Roxana was expecting were named joint kings, with Perdiccas as regent. The provinces were shared out among senior officers as satraps, setting the stage for the wars of the Diadochi (successors).

events.text: Philip III Arrhidaeus executed; Alexander IV is sole king
events.detail: After Perdiccas was murdered in 321 or 320 BCE, the veteran general Antipater became regent and took the two kings to Macedon. When he died in 319 he passed over his own son Cassander in favour of Polyperchon, and civil war broke out. Philip III's ambitious wife Eurydice sided with Cassander, while Polyperchon allied with Olympias, Alexander's mother. When Olympias invaded Macedon in 317, Eurydice's soldiers refused to fight the mother of Alexander and changed sides. Philip and Eurydice were captured and put to death, leaving the boy Alexander IV as sole king under Olympias's control.

events.text: Cassander has Alexander IV murdered, ending the Argead line
events.detail: Cassander struck back and retook Macedon in 316 BCE. He executed Olympias and held the young Alexander IV and his mother Roxana under guard in the citadel of Amphipolis. The peace of 311 promised that Alexander would succeed Cassander when he came of age, which made the boy a threat to Cassander's own power. Cassander had mother and son killed, poisoned according to the writer Pausanias, though the year is uncertain, with estimates from 311 to 304 BCE. With the last legitimate Argead king gone, nothing remained to hold Alexander's empire together.

events.text: Antigonus and Demetrius take royal titles; other generals follow
events.detail: With no Argead king left, the generals who held Alexander's provinces no longer needed to pretend to serve the royal family. In 306 BCE Demetrius, son of Antigonus the One-Eyed, destroyed Ptolemy's fleet off Salamis in Cyprus, and after this victory Antigonus and Demetrius both took the title of king. Ptolemy, Seleucus and Lysimachus soon did the same, and eventually Cassander. Alexander's empire had become a set of rival kingdoms whose rulers claimed royal rank in their own right, while Antigonus still hoped to rule it all.

events.text: Ipsus: Seleucus and Lysimachus defeat and kill Antigonus; empire divided
events.detail: Antigonus, master of most of Asia Minor and Syria, was the strongest of the successors and the last who aimed to rule Alexander's whole empire. Cassander, Lysimachus and Seleucus joined forces against him, and in 301 BCE they met Antigonus and his son Demetrius near Ipsus in Phrygia. Seleucus's war elephants, obtained from Chandragupta Maurya, cut Demetrius's cavalry off from the battle, and Antigonus was surrounded and killed by javelins. The victors carved up his lands: Ptolemy kept Egypt, Seleucus gained northern Syria and eastern Asia Minor, and Lysimachus the rest of Asia Minor. Alexander's empire was permanently divided.

reigns.name: Philip III Arrhidaeus and Alexander IV (regents Perdiccas, Antipater, Polyperchon)
Rival Diadochi kings (Antigonus, Ptolemy, Seleucus, Cassander, Lysimachus)

name: Maurya Empire
summary: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda dynasty of Magadha c. 321 BCE and, after war with Seleucus I, won the lands up to the Hindu Kush. Bindusara pushed into the Deccan and Ashoka conquered Kalinga c. 261 BCE, ruling nearly all of South Asia except the far south before turning to Buddhism. After Ashoka's death in 232 BCE weaker kings followed, and the general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last, Brihadratha, c. 185 BCE.

events.text: Chandragupta overthrows the Nandas; Pataliputra becomes the capital
events.detail: Alexander's invasion and early death left north-western India in turmoil. A young leader, Chandragupta Maurya, helped according to later tradition by his mentor Chanakya, rose against the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha in the Ganges valley. He besieged and took the Nanda capital, Pataliputra (near modern Patna), and made it his own; the conquest is usually dated c. 322–319 BCE, though the order of events is debated. He also drove out the Greek garrisons Alexander had left in the Punjab, and by about 317 BCE his new empire reached from the Ganges basin to the Indus.

events.text: War with Seleucus I begins (305–303 BCE)
events.detail: Seleucus I, who had won the eastern half of Alexander's empire, wanted to recover the Indian provinces that Alexander had conquered. Sometime between 305 and 303 BCE he crossed the Indus to fight Chandragupta, whose army, it was said, could number hundreds of thousands of men and thousands of war elephants. Almost nothing is known about the fighting: the Greek writers name no clear victor, and no Indian source mentions the war at all. What is clear is that Seleucus did not win back the Indus lands, and chose to negotiate with his powerful neighbour instead.

events.text: Peace: Seleucus cedes eastern lands for 500 war elephants
events.detail: The war ended in a treaty, usually dated c. 303–302 BCE. Seleucus handed Chandragupta his easternmost satrapies, certainly Gandhara, the Paropamisadae and eastern Gedrosia, and possibly also Arachosia and Aria, and in return received 500 war elephants with their drivers. A marriage alliance was agreed as well, probably Chandragupta marrying a daughter of Seleucus, and the Greek envoy Megasthenes later lived at the Mauryan court. The Mauryan frontier moved west into what is now Afghanistan, while the elephants helped Seleucus win the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE.

events.text: Bindusara succeeds and extends rule into the Deccan
events.detail: After Chandragupta's reign ended c. 298 BCE, his son Bindusara inherited an empire stretching across northern India. Greek writers called him Amitrochates, probably from a Sanskrit title meaning 'slayer of enemies'. A 16th-century Tibetan author claims his minister destroyed the kings of 16 towns and made him master of the land between the eastern and western seas. Some historians read this as a conquest of the Deccan, while others think Bindusara only crushed revolts and kept what his father had won. He also kept up friendly ties with the Seleucids, whose ambassador Deimachos lived at his court.

events.text: Ashoka becomes emperor
events.detail: Before becoming emperor, Bindusara's son Ashoka served as a royal governor, at Ujjain or in Gandhara according to different traditions, and is said to have put down a revolt at Taxila. Buddhist legends claim that his succession was disputed and that he killed his eldest brother, even 99 half-brothers, to take the throne, but these stories cannot be confirmed. He became emperor around 269–268 BCE, ruling from Pataliputra. His empire covered most of the Indian subcontinent, from present-day Afghanistan in the west to present-day Bangladesh in the east.

events.text: Kalinga War; its carnage turns Ashoka towards Buddhism
events.detail: Kalinga was an independent kingdom on India's east coast, in present-day Odisha, whose ports and navy controlled trade across the Bay of Bengal. In his eighth regnal year, c. 261 BCE (some date it to c. 260), Ashoka conquered it in one of the largest and deadliest wars in Indian history. His own edict records that 150,000 people were deported and 100,000 killed, with many more dying afterwards, and says he felt 'deep remorse'. Kalinga was added to the empire, but Ashoka turned away from conquest towards dhamma (righteous conduct) and, gradually, Buddhism.

events.text: Ashoka dies; a series of weaker rulers follows
events.detail: Ashoka spent the rest of his reign promoting dhamma through edicts carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, and sent envoys westward to the Hellenistic kingdoms. When he died in 232 BCE, none of his sons took the throne; his grandson Dasharatha succeeded him. For about 50 years a series of weaker emperors followed, and the empire may have been divided in two. Many territories were lost under Dasharatha and partly regained by Samprati, but after him the Mauryas slowly lost more and more land, and the empire on the map shrinks back towards Magadha.

events.text: Pushyamitra Shunga assassinates Brihadratha, ending the dynasty
events.detail: By the early 2nd century BCE the Mauryan realm had shrunk to its heartland around Pataliputra, while the Greco-Bactrian king Demetrius was invading the north-west. Brihadratha, the last Maurya emperor, was assassinated by his own army commander, Pushyamitra Shunga, during a military parade, according to a later literary account. The killing is usually dated 185 BCE, though some put it as late as 180. Pushyamitra founded the Shunga Empire in the old Mauryan heartland of the Ganges valley, while the Indo-Greeks took over the north-west: the Maurya Empire had come to an end.

name: Seleucid Empire
summary: Seleucus I took Babylon in 312 BCE and, after Ipsus and Corupedium, ruled from the Aegean to the borders of India. Bactria and Parthia broke away in the mid-3rd century; Antiochus III restored much of the realm but lost Anatolia to Rome after Magnesia (190 BCE), and the Parthians took Mesopotamia in 141 BCE. Reduced to Syria and torn by dynastic wars, the kingdom was annexed by Pompey in 63 BCE.

events.text: Seleucus takes Babylon; the Seleucid era begins
events.detail: After Alexander's death his officer Seleucus became satrap of Babylonia in 321 BCE, but Antigonus the One-Eyed, the most powerful of the successors, forced him to flee to Ptolemy in Egypt. In 312 BCE Seleucus helped Ptolemy defeat Antigonus's son Demetrius at Gaza and then returned to Babylon, arriving by spring 311 according to some accounts. His court later counted years from this return as the Seleucid era, whose first year began in autumn 312 BCE by Macedonian reckoning. Holding Babylon, Seleucus could now build a kingdom across the eastern half of Alexander's empire.

events.text: Seleucus takes the royal title; war with Chandragupta Maurya (305–303)
events.detail: From Babylon Seleucus defeated Antigonus's forces and took Persia and Media, until he ruled the whole eastern part of Alexander's empire. After Antigonus and Demetrius proclaimed themselves kings in 306 BCE, Seleucus too took the title of king (basileus). He then marched to the Indus to recover Alexander's Indian satrapies, but Chandragupta Maurya had already taken them. The war (305–303 BCE) is poorly recorded and ended in a treaty: Seleucus ceded his easternmost provinces, in parts of today's Afghanistan and Pakistan, in return for 500 war elephants and a marriage alliance.

events.text: Ipsus: Seleucus gains northern Syria and eastern Anatolia
events.detail: With his eastern frontier settled, Seleucus marched west with his elephants to join Lysimachus and Cassander against Antigonus, the strongest of Alexander's successors. At Ipsus in Phrygia in 301 BCE the elephants kept Demetrius's cavalry from returning to the fight, and Antigonus was killed. In the division that followed, Seleucus took eastern Anatolia and northern Syria. There he founded a new capital, Antioch on the Orontes, named after his father, alongside Seleucia on the Tigris in Mesopotamia. The empire now reached the Mediterranean coast, and Syria would become its heartland.

events.text: Victory at Corupedium brings the widest extent; Seleucus is assassinated
events.detail: Lysimachus, who ruled Thrace, western Asia Minor and, recently, Macedon, had his own heir Agathocles murdered, and the crisis drew him into war with Seleucus. In 281 BCE their armies met at Corupedium in Lydia, and Lysimachus died in the fighting, killed by a javelin according to one ancient account. The victory gave Seleucus nominal control of almost all of Alexander's empire except Egypt, from western Anatolia to the borders of India. But when he crossed into Europe to claim Thrace and Macedon, he was assassinated by Ptolemy Ceraunus, and Macedon became independent again.

events.text: Bactria and then Parthia break away in the mid-3rd century
events.detail: Under Antiochus II and his son Seleucus II the empire was weakened by wars against Ptolemaic Egypt and by a civil war between Seleucus II and his brother Antiochus Hierax. Taking advantage, the governors of the far east broke away: Diodotus in Bactria declared independence around 245 BCE (the date is very uncertain), founding the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, and Andragoras did the same in Parthia. Soon after, c. 238, the nomad chief Arsaces invaded Parthia and founded the Arsacid dynasty. The empire lost its north-eastern provinces, and Parthia would grow into its deadliest rival.

events.text: Antiochus III defeated by Ptolemy IV at Raphia
events.detail: Ptolemaic Egypt and the Seleucids fought a long series of Syrian Wars over Coele-Syria, the southern Levant. In the Fourth Syrian War, which began in 219 BCE, the young Antiochus III overran much of the region. On 22 June 217 BCE he met Ptolemy IV near Raphia (modern Rafah) in one of the largest battles of the ancient world: by Polybius's figures, 70,000 infantry and 73 African elephants against 62,000 infantry and 102 Indian elephants. Antiochus's elephants won their duel, but his army was beaten, and he had to give up his conquests and withdraw north of Lebanon.

events.text: Antiochus III's eastern campaign reaches the Kabul valley
events.detail: After Raphia, Antiochus III set out to restore Seleucid power in the east. In 209 BCE he invaded Parthia and took its capital Hecatompylos, and King Arsaces II apparently sued for peace. In Bactria he defeated Euthydemus I but could not take the capital Bactra, so he made an honourable peace that let Euthydemus keep his royal title. Following in Alexander's footsteps, he then crossed into the Kabul valley, renewed his friendship with the Indian king Sophagasenus and received more elephants, returning west c. 206–205 BCE. The campaign brought the east back under Seleucid supremacy and earned him the name 'the Great'.

events.text: Antiochus III wins at Panium and takes Coele-Syria from the Ptolemies
events.detail: Coele-Syria had been fought over by the Seleucids and Ptolemies for a century. In 202 BCE its Ptolemaic governor defected to Antiochus III, who overran most of the province, including Gaza, by autumn 201. After the Aetolian general Scopas retook parts of it for Egypt, Antiochus brought him to battle in summer 200 BCE at Panium, near Mount Hermon, and annihilated the Ptolemaic army; some modern accounts date the battle to 198. Coele-Syria passed to the Seleucids, and the Ptolemaic kingdom never again acted as an independent great power.

events.text: Rome crushes Antiochus III at Magnesia
events.detail: Antiochus III next expanded into Thrace and, encouraged by the Aetolian League, crossed into Greece in 192 BCE, bringing him into war with Rome. Beaten at Thermopylae in 191, he retreated to Asia Minor, where a Roman army under the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with King Eumenes II of Pergamon, met him near Magnesia ad Sipylum. In the battle, fought in December 190 or January 189 BCE, Eumenes broke the Seleucid left and the centre collapsed while Antiochus was away pursuing on the right with his cavalry. The defeat shattered Seleucid power in the west.

events.text: Treaty of Apamea: all land north and west of the Taurus surrendered
events.detail: The peace Rome imposed at Apamea in 188 BCE was harsh. Antiochus III had to abandon Europe and all of Asia Minor west of the Taurus Mountains, lands that Rome handed to its allies Pergamon and Rhodes. He had to surrender all his war elephants and keep none in future, limit his navy to twelve warships, give twenty hostages including one of his sons, and pay 15,000 talents of silver over twelve years. The Seleucids lost their Anatolian provinces for good, and the heavy payments strained the treasury for years.

events.text: Parthians under Mithridates I take Seleucia and Mesopotamia
events.detail: After Antiochus IV died in 164 BCE, rival Seleucid claimants fought repeated civil wars, and the Parthian king Mithridates I seized his chance. He invaded Media and took Ecbatana in 148 or 147 BCE, then conquered Babylonia; in 141 he was minting coins at Seleucia on the Tigris, Seleucus's old eastern capital, and held a formal investiture there. When Demetrius II tried to win back the east, he was defeated and captured in 139. By then the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia were Parthian, and the Seleucid kingdom was shrinking towards Syria.

events.text: Antiochus VII defeated and killed by the Parthians at Ecbatana
events.detail: Demetrius II's brother Antiochus VII Sidetes, sometimes called the last great Seleucid king, restored order in Syria and then marched east with the last great royal army, winning three battles and recovering Mesopotamia, Babylonia and Media. In the winter of 130–129 BCE his troops were spread out in winter quarters, and local people, angry at having to feed them, rose in revolt. The Parthian king Phraates II attacked, and Antiochus was killed in 129, at a battle near Ecbatana in some accounts or in an ambush in the Zagros in others. All the recovered lands returned to Parthia, and the kingdom was reduced to Syria.

events.text: Tigranes of Armenia takes Syria
events.detail: After Antiochus VII's death, rival members of the dynasty fought one another for decades, and the kingdom shrank to a handful of Syrian cities. In 83 BCE, tired of the bloody strife, the Syrians offered their crown to Tigranes the Great of Armenia, who placed a governor in Antioch and went on to conquer Phoenicia and Cilicia, reaching as far south as Ptolemais (Acre). This effectively ended the Seleucid state, although a few cities still recognised a boy-king of the dynasty. Syria stayed under Armenian rule until the Roman general Lucullus defeated Tigranes in 69 BCE.

events.text: Pompey makes Syria a Roman province
events.detail: After Lucullus's victory a rump Seleucid kingdom was restored under Antiochus XIII, but a rival Seleucid, Philip II, contested his rule, and Syria remained unstable. Rome, now dominant in the East after its wars against Mithridates of Pontus, grew alarmed at the disorder. The general Pompey annexed Syria and its wealthy cities in 64 BCE (63 in some accounts) and organised them as a new Roman province, before moving south to Damascus and Judea. The last remnant of the empire of Seleucus, which had once stretched to India, disappeared from the map.

reigns.name: Rival claimants (Demetrius II to Antiochus XIII)

name: Ptolemaic Kingdom
summary: Ptolemy I, Alexander's satrap in Egypt from 323 BCE, made himself king in 305 BCE and added Cyrenaica, Cyprus and Coele-Syria; under Ptolemy III in the 240s the kingdom reached its height, campaigning as far as Babylonia. Native revolts, the loss of Coele-Syria (200 BCE) and dynastic feuds weakened it as Rome's influence grew; Cleopatra VII's defeat at Actium led to Egypt's annexation by Rome in 30 BCE.

events.text: Ptolemy I declares himself king, ruling from Alexandria
events.detail: After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, his general Ptolemy became satrap (governor) of Egypt, nominally serving Alexander's heirs while building his own power. He beat off an invasion by the regent Perdiccas in 321 BCE and, during the wars between Alexander's successors, won Cyrenaica, Cyprus and Coele-Syria. When Antigonus and Demetrius took royal titles in 306 BCE, Ptolemy followed and proclaimed himself king in 305/304 BCE, ruling from Alexander's new city of Alexandria. Egypt became an independent Greek-ruled kingdom, and his dynasty would hold it for nearly three centuries.

events.text: Ptolemy III's Third Syrian War reaches Babylonia: the kingdom's height
events.detail: Ptolemy III came to the throne in 246 BCE just as a succession crisis broke out in the rival Seleucid Empire. His sister Berenice, widow of the Seleucid king Antiochus II, was murdered with her infant son, and Ptolemy went to war against her rival's son, Seleucus II. In this Third Syrian War (246–241 BCE) he won victories in Syria and Anatolia, briefly held Antioch and, as a cuneiform tablet shows, even reached Babylon, while his fleets made conquests as far as Thrace. This was the height of Ptolemaic power, with Egypt controlling most of the coasts of the eastern Mediterranean.

events.text: Ptolemy IV defeats Antiochus III at Raphia
events.detail: Antiochus III, the energetic young Seleucid king, wanted to win back Coele-Syria, the strip of land between Egypt and Syria that the Ptolemies had held for about eighty years. On 22 June 217 BCE the two kings met near Raphia (modern Rafah) in one of the largest battles of the Hellenistic age; Polybius gives about 70,000 infantry for Ptolemy IV and 62,000 for Antiochus. Antiochus's Indian elephants scattered Ptolemy's smaller African ones, but the Ptolemaic phalanx, in which native Egyptian soldiers played a major role, won the day. Coele-Syria stayed Egyptian, but the war strained the treasury and boosted native Egyptian confidence.

events.text: Great Theban Revolt breaks out in Upper Egypt
events.detail: Under Ptolemy IV, misrule from Alexandria and the financial strain of war bred deep resentment among native Egyptians, especially in the south, far from the Greek capital. In 205 BCE a priest named Horwennefer proclaimed himself pharaoh, and rebels seized Thebes and much of Upper Egypt. After his death in 199 BCE his son Ankhwennefer carried on the fight, at times nearly driving the Ptolemies out of the country. For about twenty years the kings in Alexandria lost control of much of Egypt, just as foreign enemies were preparing to attack their overseas lands.

events.text: Coele-Syria lost to the Seleucids
events.detail: When Ptolemy IV died, his heir Ptolemy V was a small child ruled by regents, and the Great Revolt was still raging in the south. Antiochus III of the Seleucid Empire and Philip V of Macedon agreed to seize the Ptolemies' overseas possessions: Philip took islands and towns in Caria and Thrace, while Antiochus invaded Coele-Syria. At the Battle of Panium in 200 BCE Antiochus defeated the Ptolemaic army and took Coele-Syria and Judea. Egypt's lands in the Levant passed to the Seleucids, and the weakened kingdom turned to an alliance with the rising power of Rome.

events.text: Theban revolt finally suppressed
events.detail: The native revolt in Upper Egypt, led since 199 BCE by Ankhwennefer, had dragged on for nearly twenty years and at times threatened to end Greek rule altogether. In 186 BCE the forces of the young Ptolemy V finally defeated the rebel dynasty and restored royal control over Thebes and the south. Egypt was reunited under one king again, and the Ptolemies kept courting the powerful Egyptian priesthood with gifts and temple building. But the long war had severely weakened their hold on the country, and the kingdom never fully recovered its earlier strength.

events.text: Day of Eleusis: Rome orders Antiochus IV out of Egypt and Cyprus
events.detail: In the Sixth Syrian War (170–168 BCE) the Seleucid king Antiochus IV invaded Egypt, captured the young Ptolemy VI and set him up as a puppet king at Memphis, while Alexandria crowned his brother instead. In 168 BCE Antiochus invaded again, seized Cyprus and Memphis, and marched on Alexandria. At Eleusis, a suburb of the capital, the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas handed him the Senate's order to leave Egypt and Cyprus; according to Polybius, he drew a circle in the sand around the king and demanded an answer before he stepped out. Antiochus obeyed, so Egypt survived, but as a kingdom that now owed its independence to Rome.

events.text: Death of Ptolemy VI; decades of dynastic feuding follow
events.detail: Ptolemy VI Philometor had restored some strength, reasserting control over northern Nubia and intervening in the Seleucid civil wars in Syria. In 145 BCE he was killed in the Battle of Antioch, and his infant son was soon murdered by his uncle, who seized the throne as Ptolemy VIII. For more than a century afterwards, members of the dynasty fought one another: kings were driven out and restored, and one, Ptolemy XI, was lynched by the Alexandrian mob. These feuds left Egypt so weak that it became in effect a protectorate of Rome.

events.text: Ptolemy Apion dies and bequeaths Cyrenaica to Rome
events.detail: Cyrenaica, the fertile coast of eastern Libya, had belonged to the Ptolemies since Ptolemy I, but at times it was ruled separately by rival members of the dynasty. Ptolemy Apion, an illegitimate son of Ptolemy VIII, was apparently given Cyrene as his own kingdom around 105–101 BCE, although almost nothing is recorded of his reign and some scholars doubt he ruled at all. When he died without heirs in 96 BCE, his will left Cyrenaica and his royal estates to the Roman Republic. The Ptolemaic realm shrank to Egypt and Cyprus, and Rome now stood on Egypt's western border.

events.text: Cleopatra VII comes to the throne
events.detail: Cleopatra's father, Ptolemy XII Auletes, had kept his throne by paying vast sums to Rome and was even restored by the Romans after the Alexandrian mob drove him out in 58 BCE. When he died in 51 BCE, his will, with the Roman Senate as executor, left the kingdom jointly to Cleopatra VII, then in her late teens, and her 10-year-old brother Ptolemy XIII. Cleopatra soon fell out with her brother's advisers, was driven into exile and regained power only with Julius Caesar's help in 48–47 BCE. She would be the last ruler of an independent Egypt, trying to restore Ptolemaic power through alliances with Roman leaders.

events.text: Antony and Cleopatra defeated by Octavian at Actium
events.detail: Cleopatra's partner Mark Antony and Octavian, Caesar's heir, had shared the Roman world, but by 32 BCE their rivalry turned into war, which Rome declared on Cleopatra. Octavian's admiral Agrippa cut Antony's supply lines in western Greece and trapped his army and fleet at Actium. On 2 September 31 BCE Antony's fleet tried to break out but was routed by Octavian's smaller, more agile ships, and Antony and Cleopatra escaped to Egypt. Their army in Greece deserted or surrendered, leaving Egypt with no real defence against a Roman invasion.

events.text: Cleopatra dies; Egypt becomes a Roman province
events.detail: In the summer of 30 BCE Octavian's forces invaded Egypt and beat Antony's remaining troops outside Alexandria, and Antony killed himself. Cleopatra, unwilling to be paraded in a Roman triumph, took her own life in August 30 BCE, by tradition through the bite of an asp, though poison is more likely. Octavian had her son by Caesar, Caesarion, executed and made Egypt a Roman province. The Ptolemaic Kingdom, the last independent Hellenistic state, vanished from the map, and Egypt's grain and wealth now served Rome.

name: Parthian Empire
summary: Arsaces I, leader of the Parni, founded the Arsacid state in Parthia c. 247 BCE; Mithridates I (c. 171–132 BCE) took Media and Mesopotamia from the Seleucids, and Mithridates II extended Parthian power from the Euphrates to Afghanistan. Astride the Silk Road, Parthia fought Rome for three centuries, destroying Crassus at Carrhae but losing Ctesiphon to Trajan, Avidius Cassius and Severus. Weakened by civil war, the last king, Artabanus IV, fell to Ardashir I of Persis in 224 CE.

events.text: Arsaces I begins the Arsacid era
events.detail: Arsaces I was chief of the Parni, a nomadic Iranian people of the Dahae confederation on the steppes north-east of Iran. Around this time the Seleucid governor of Parthia, Andragoras, rebelled against his king, and the Parni went on to conquer the province, probably overthrowing Andragoras in about 238 BCE. The Arsacid kings later counted their era from 247 BCE, although historians disagree about what actually happened that year. From this small base in north-east Iran grew an empire that would rule from the Euphrates to Afghanistan for almost five centuries.

events.text: Mithridates I conquers Media
events.detail: For decades the Parthians held only north-eastern Iran, but Mithridates I (c. 171–132 BCE), whom one historian compares to Cyrus the Great, turned the kingdom into an empire. After seizing two provinces from the Greco-Bactrian kingdom to the east, he turned on the Seleucids, whose hold on Media had just been shaken by the rebellion of Timarchus. In 148 or 147 BCE he invaded Media and occupied its capital, Ecbatana (modern Hamadan). Parthia now held the western Iranian plateau and the road down to Mesopotamia, and Ecbatana became the kings' summer residence.

events.text: Mithridates I takes Seleucia and Mesopotamia
events.detail: With Media secured, Mithridates I pushed down into Babylonia, the rich lowland heart of the Seleucid east. By 141 BCE he was minting coins at Seleucia on the Tigris, the great Greek city of Mesopotamia, and held an official investiture ceremony there. His forces then subdued Elymais and Characene and occupied Susa, and a Seleucid counter-attack ended with King Demetrius II taken prisoner. Parthian authority now ran from Mesopotamia as far east as the Indus, and Ctesiphon, across the river from Seleucia, would later become the royal capital.

events.text: Phraates II defeats and kills the Seleucid Antiochus VII at Ecbatana
events.detail: The Seleucid king Antiochus VII set out in 130 BCE to win back Mesopotamia, defeating a Parthian general on the Great Zab and occupying Babylonia and Susa. He demanded that Phraates II give up everything except Parthia itself and pay heavy tribute. But his army wintered in Media and exhausted the countryside, and in spring 129 BCE the Medes revolted; the main Parthian army then attacked and killed Antiochus at the Battle of Ecbatana. It was the last great Seleucid attempt to recover the east: Mesopotamia remained Parthian, and the Seleucid kingdom shrank back to Syria.

events.text: Mithridates II begins a reign of expansion; Armenia forced to submit
events.detail: Victory over the Seleucids was followed by disaster in the east, where Saka nomads, pushed west by the Yuezhi, killed Phraates II and, according to Justin, his successor Artabanus I. Mithridates II (c. 124–91 BCE) restored the empire: he recovered lands lost to the Saka, made the kings of Characene his vassals and occupied Dura-Europos on the Euphrates in 113 BCE. In 97 BCE his forces deposed Artavasdes I of Armenia and took the young prince Tigranes hostage. Parthian power now reached from the Euphrates to Afghanistan, and a Parthian envoy met Rome's Sulla on the Euphrates.

events.text: Surena destroys Crassus's Roman army at Carrhae
events.detail: Marcus Licinius Crassus, one of Rome's three ruling triumvirs and now governor of Syria, invaded Mesopotamia in 53 BCE. Near Carrhae (modern Harran in Turkey), his seven legions met the Parthian general Surena, whose army was entirely mounted: about 1,000 armoured cataphracts and 9,000 horse archers, kept supplied with arrows by a camel train. Though outnumbered roughly four to one, the Parthians shot the Roman infantry to pieces; some 20,000 Romans died, about 10,000 were captured, and Crassus was killed at a parley. It was one of Rome's worst defeats, and it fixed Parthia's reputation as Rome's equal in the east.

events.text: Parthian forces overrun most of the Levant (40–39 BCE)
events.detail: After Carrhae the Parthians tried to seize Rome's eastern provinces, and Rome's civil wars gave them their chance. In 40–39 BCE the crown prince Pacorus I, joined by the renegade Roman general Quintus Labienus, overran Syria; Labienus pushed into Anatolia while Pacorus took every city on the Levantine coast as far south as Ptolemais (Acre) except Tyre. In Judea they made their ally Antigonus king, and Herod fled. For a short time Parthian power reached the Mediterranean, until Mark Antony's general Ventidius drove them back, killing Pacorus at Mount Gindarus in 38 BCE.

events.text: Mark Antony invades Parthia and suffers heavy losses
events.detail: Phraates IV had secured the Parthian throne by killing or exiling his brothers, and one of them, Monaeses, persuaded Mark Antony to invade. In 36 BCE Antony led a huge army, put at 90,000–100,000 men with his allies, through Armenia into Media Atropatene (north-west Iran) and besieged its capital. Parthian cavalry destroyed his slow siege train, the Armenian king abandoned him, and the siege failed. On the long retreat, harassed all the way, Antony lost tens of thousands of men, though the ancient accounts disagree widely on the numbers. Parthia's territory remained intact.

events.text: Trajan captures Ctesiphon
events.detail: Rome and Parthia had long competed to control Armenia, and when the Parthian king Osroes I installed his own candidate there without consulting Rome, Emperor Trajan went to war. In 114 CE he made Armenia a Roman province, and in 115 he invaded Mesopotamia, meeting little resistance because Osroes was fighting a civil war in the east. In 116 Trajan marched down the Euphrates, took Dura-Europos, Seleucia and the capital Ctesiphon, and reached the Persian Gulf. Never again would the Roman Empire advance so far east, and for a moment Parthia's western heartland was in Roman hands.

events.text: Trajan withdraws; the Euphrates frontier is restored
events.detail: Trajan's conquests proved fragile. While he was in the south, the cities of Babylonia rose against their Roman garrisons, and on his way north he failed to take the desert fortress of Hatra. In 117 CE he withdrew from Mesopotamia, intending to return the next year, but he died suddenly in August. His successor Hadrian, short of troops, chose not to hold Mesopotamia and confirmed the Euphrates as the frontier. Parthia regained its lowland heartland, though the war had shown how exposed Ctesiphon was to Roman armies marching down the rivers.

events.text: Avidius Cassius invades; Seleucia and Ctesiphon burned
events.detail: In 161 CE the Parthian king Vologases IV invaded Armenia and Syria, starting a new war with Rome. The co-emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus struck back: one army invaded Armenia in 163, and in 164 (some accounts say 165) the general Avidius Cassius led another down into Mesopotamia. The Romans captured Seleucia and Ctesiphon and burned them to the ground, but a deadly epidemic, possibly smallpox, broke out among the soldiers and forced them to retreat. Rome kept Dura-Europos on the middle Euphrates, and Parthia's great Mesopotamian cities lay in ruins.

events.text: Septimius Severus captures Seleucia and Ctesiphon
events.detail: Septimius Severus had just won Rome's civil war, and Parthia and its vassals had backed his rival Pescennius Niger. In 197 CE, during the reign of Vologases V, Severus crossed the Euphrates and, like Trajan, marched his army down the river to capture Seleucia and sack Ctesiphon, probably late in 197 or early in 198. He took the title Parthicus Maximus but, again like Trajan, failed to take Hatra after two long sieges. Rome annexed the northern half of Mesopotamia, pushing its frontier deeper into former Parthian lands.

events.text: Artabanus IV rebels against Vologases VI: civil war
events.detail: Around 212–213 CE, a few years after Vologases VI succeeded his father, his brother Artabanus IV rebelled and took most of the empire, including Media and Susa, while Vologases kept a small realm around Seleucia. The Roman emperor Caracalla exploited the split, invading Mesopotamia and sacking the Parthian royal tombs at Arbela. Artabanus fought the Romans off at Nisibis in 217, and Rome paid a large indemnity for peace. But the long civil war drained Arsacid strength just as a new power was rising in Persis in the south-west.

events.text: Ardashir I defeats and kills Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan
events.detail: In Persis (modern Fars), the local prince Ardashir I of the Sasanian family had begun conquering neighbouring regions such as Kerman in defiance of Arsacid rule. When Artabanus IV finally marched against him, the two armies met at Hormozdgan, a site still not located, on 28 April 224 CE; Artabanus was defeated and killed. Ardashir took the title King of Kings, and his Sasanian Empire replaced the Parthians across Iran and Mesopotamia, although Vologases VI held out at Seleucia until about 228. Almost five centuries of Arsacid rule had ended.

name: Qin and Han China
summary: The state of Qin conquered its last rivals in 221 BCE and its king became the First Emperor, standardising script, coinage and law, but the dynasty collapsed in revolts soon after his death and ended in 206 BCE. Liu Bang founded the Han in 202 BCE; under Emperor Wu (141–87 BCE) it drove back the Xiongnu and expanded into Central Asia, Korea and the far south. After Wang Mang's Xin interlude (9–23 CE) the Eastern Han ruled from Luoyang until rebellion and warlords ended it in 220 CE.

events.text: Qin conquers Qi, its last rival; King Zheng becomes the First Emperor
events.detail: For centuries the Warring States had fought for supremacy while the old Zhou kings faded into figureheads, and Qin, secure in the mountain-ringed Guanzhong basin in the west, had built the most efficient army and state. From 230 BCE King Zheng conquered the six remaining states one by one: Han, Zhao, Yan, Wei, Chu and finally Qi, whose capital Linzi fell in 221 BCE. He took the new title Shi Huangdi, 'First Emperor', and governed through appointed officials instead of royal relatives. For the first time the Chinese heartland, from the Yellow River plains to the Yangtze, was a single empire.

events.text: Meng Tian takes the Ordos region from the Xiongnu
events.detail: Xiongnu herders in the Ordos, the grassland inside the great northern loop of the Yellow River, often raided Qin farmers. The First Emperor sent General Meng Tian north with an army said to number 300,000, and in 215 BCE he expelled the Xiongnu from the Ordos and drove them back onto the Mongolian Plateau. Qin settled farmers in the region and began the long chain of defences later remembered as the Great Wall. The empire's northern frontier now enclosed the Ordos, but after Qin fell the Xiongnu leader Modu retook it.

events.text: Qin Shi Huang dies on tour; Huhai is made Second Emperor
events.detail: Obsessed with immortality, the First Emperor died in 210 BCE while touring the eastern frontier, reportedly while seeking an elixir of eternal life. His chief eunuch Zhao Gao and chancellor Li Si hid his death, forged an order telling the heir, Prince Fusu, to kill himself, and had General Meng Tian put to death. They placed a younger son, Huhai, on the throne as the Second Emperor, hoping to rule through him. Huhai's purges, building projects and higher taxes soon set off revolts across the empire, and the newly united realm began to break apart.

events.text: Xianyang destroyed after Ziying's surrender: the Qin dynasty ends
events.detail: Rebellions spread from 209 BCE, and rebel leaders declared themselves kings of the old states. In 207 BCE Zhao Gao forced the Second Emperor to kill himself and installed Ziying, who ruled only as a king; Ziying had Zhao Gao killed but, after just 46 days, surrendered to the rebel general Liu Bang when he reached the capital, Xianyang. The Chu leader Xiang Yu then had Ziying executed and Xianyang destroyed in 206 BCE. The Qin dynasty ended after only 15 years, and its empire split into some eighteen rival kingdoms.

events.text: Liu Bang defeats Xiang Yu at Gaixia and founds the Han dynasty
events.detail: After Qin fell, Xiang Yu of Chu made himself overlord and gave Liu Bang, a man of humble birth, the small fief of Hanzhong. War between the two, the Chu–Han Contention, followed for four years. In the winter of 203–202 BCE Liu Bang's armies trapped Xiang Yu at Gaixia and destroyed his army, and Xiang Yu killed himself by the Wu River. A few months later Liu Bang proclaimed himself emperor of a new dynasty named Han, after his old fief; with one brief break, it would rule China for four centuries.

events.text: Xiongnu trap the emperor at Baideng; a heqin truce follows (198)
events.detail: Modu Chanyu had united the Xiongnu into a powerful steppe empire, and when a Han vassal king, Xin, defected to him, they captured Jinyang in the north. Emperor Gaozu led a large army to drive them back, but near Pingcheng (modern Datong) he and his vanguard were surrounded on Mount Baideng and cut off for seven days. He escaped, reportedly after his envoys persuaded Modu's wife to urge a withdrawal. In 198 BCE the Han agreed the heqin treaty, sending a princess and gifts of silk, food and wine, and until the 130s BCE they bought peace on the northern frontier rather than fighting.

events.text: Rebellion of the Seven States crushed; regional kings weakened
events.detail: Liu Bang had given his relatives large semi-independent kingdoms covering a third to a half of the empire, and by the 150s BCE princes such as Liu Pi of Wu minted coins, collected taxes and largely ignored the court. When Emperor Jing, advised by Chao Cuo, began cutting their lands, seven kings rose in revolt in 154 BCE. The imperial general Zhou Yafu let the loyal kingdom of Liang absorb the rebel attack while his cavalry cut their supply lines, and the revolt was crushed within three months. The kingdoms were reduced and imperial power grew sharply, preparing the way for Emperor Wu's expansion.

events.text: Battle of Mobei drives the Xiongnu north of the Gobi
events.detail: After years of Han offensives under Emperor Wu, the Xiongnu chanyu Yizhixie pulled his people north of the Gobi Desert, hoping the barren land would protect them. In early 119 BCE Wu sent two columns of 50,000 cavalry each, backed by over 140,000 infantry and supply troops, across the desert under Wei Qing and Huo Qubing. Wei Qing routed the chanyu's army in a sandstorm, while Huo Qubing crushed the eastern Xiongnu and pushed far north, reportedly as far as Lake Baikal. The Xiongnu lost much of their manpower and livestock and were driven from the lands south of the Gobi, though Han lost some 80 per cent of its horses in a decade of war.

events.text: Han conquers Nanyue in the far south
events.detail: As Qin collapsed, Zhao Tuo, a former Qin officer, had set himself up as king of Nanyue, covering modern Guangdong, Guangxi and northern Vietnam. In 113 BCE Nanyue's queen dowager, herself Chinese, proposed accepting Han overlordship, but the minister Lü Jia led the opposition and in 112 BCE had her executed. Emperor Wu sent six armies by sea, overland and down the Xi River, and in 111 BCE the capital Panyu (modern Guangzhou) fell and Nanyue surrendered. Han set up nine commanderies there, pushing its southern frontier to northern Vietnam and opening sea trade with Southeast Asia.

events.text: Han conquers Gojoseon in Korea
events.detail: Wiman Chosŏn, the kingdom of Gojoseon in northern Korea and southern Manchuria, under King Ugeo blocked envoys from other Korean chiefs from reaching the Han court. In 109 BCE Emperor Wu invaded with two forces: 50,000 men by sea across the Bohai and another army overland through Liaodong. Both suffered early defeats, and the capital Wanggeom (near modern Pyongyang) held out for months. In 108 BCE leading ministers surrendered and King Ugeo was assassinated, and Han created four commanderies in the northern half of the peninsula. The most important, Lelang, remained under Chinese control until 313 CE.

events.text: Protectorate of the Western Regions set up in the Tarim Basin
events.detail: After the wars with the Xiongnu, Han wanted to control the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim Basin, both to keep the Xiongnu away from China and to command the Silk Road trade that passed through them. In 60 or 59 BCE, after a Xiongnu prince, the Rizhu King, submitted to Han, the envoy Zheng Ji was made Protector-General of the Western Regions, overseeing both the northern and southern routes from a headquarters at Wulei near Kucha. It was the first direct rule by a Chinese government in the region. Han power now reached deep into what is today Xinjiang.

events.text: Wang Mang seizes the throne and founds the Xin dynasty
events.detail: In the last decades of the Western Han, the family of Empress Dowager Wang held the regency for a series of weak or child emperors. Her nephew Wang Mang became regent in 1 BCE and acting emperor for the infant heir Ruzi Ying in 6 CE, then in 9 CE claimed the Mandate of Heaven and founded his own Xin dynasty. His reforms, such as outlawing slavery, sharing out land and issuing new coins, met fierce opposition, and huge Yellow River floods drove peasants into rebel bands such as the Red Eyebrows. In 23 CE rebels stormed Chang'an and killed him, and Han control of the Tarim Basin was lost.

events.text: Emperor Guangwu restores the Han and moves the capital to Luoyang
events.detail: Liu Xiu, a distant descendant of the Han emperors, was one of several claimants who rose during the civil wars after Wang Mang's fall. He proclaimed himself emperor on 5 August 25 CE, taking the name Guangwu, and defeated the marauding Red Eyebrows and rival warlords, reunifying China by 36 CE. He made Luoyang, about 335 km east of the ruined Chang'an, his capital, which is why his dynasty is called the Eastern Han. His reforms gave the Han nearly two more centuries of rule over a restored empire.

events.text: Yellow Turban Rebellion; generals who crush it become warlords
events.detail: By the 180s CE the Eastern Han court was paralysed by power struggles, while peasants suffered heavy taxes and forced labour. The Taoist faith healer Zhang Jue built a vast following, the Way of Supreme Peace, and when his plot was betrayed the rising broke out early, in 184 CE, across eight provinces; the rebels wore yellow headscarves. Han armies crushed the main revolt within a year, but smaller uprisings went on until 205. Many generals raised to fight the rebels kept their troops and became warlords, and the empire's central authority never recovered.

events.text: Cao Pi takes the throne from Emperor Xian, ending the Han
events.detail: After 189 CE the warlord Dong Zhuo wrecked the Han court, and the empire split among rival warlords. Cao Cao took control of the young Emperor Xian in 196 and ruled in his name, but his drive to reunify China was stopped at the Battle of Red Cliffs in 208–209. In 220 his son Cao Pi pressured Emperor Xian to abdicate and founded the Wei dynasty, formally ending the Han. Liu Bei proclaimed the Shu Han dynasty in 221 and Sun Quan founded Wu in 222, so China was divided into the Three Kingdoms until 280.
