name: Xiongnu
summary: Modu Chanyu (209–174 BCE) united the nomads of the Mongolian Plateau into a confederation that humbled the early Han and drove the Yuezhi west. Emperor Wu's wars from 133 BCE broke Xiongnu power; a succession war ended with Huhanye submitting to Han, and in 48 CE the confederation split into Southern and Northern Xiongnu. Han campaigns in 89–91 CE destroyed the Northern state, whose chanyu fled west.

events.text: Modu kills his father Touman and becomes chanyu
events.detail: The Xiongnu were horse-riding nomads of the Mongolian Plateau, and in 215 BCE the Qin general Meng Tian had driven them out of their pastures in the Ordos. Their chief, Touman, favoured another son as heir and, according to Sima Qian, sent his eldest son Modu as a hostage to the Yuezhi, hoping he would be killed, but Modu escaped. Modu then trained his warriors to shoot wherever his whistling arrow flew, and in 209 BCE had them kill his father during a hunt. As chanyu (supreme ruler), he united the steppe tribes into a powerful confederation able to field large, coordinated armies.

events.text: Modu defeats the Yuezhi
events.detail: Having seized power, Modu turned on the Xiongnu's neighbours. By 208 BCE he had crushed the Donghu of eastern Mongolia and Manchuria, whose survivors became the Xianbei and Wuhuan peoples, and he went on to subdue the Dingling and other peoples to the north. In 203 BCE he defeated the Yuezhi, the strong nomad people of the Gansu grasslands to the south-west who had once held him hostage. After these victories all the Xiongnu lords submitted to him, and his empire spread across the eastern steppe from Manchuria towards Gansu.

events.text: Modu surrounds the Han emperor Gaozu at Baideng
events.detail: Modu had also retaken the Ordos from the collapsing Qin, and when the Han vassal king Xin defected to him, their forces raided northern China. Emperor Gaozu marched north with a huge army but pushed ahead to Pingcheng (modern Datong) with only part of it, and Modu's cavalry surrounded him on Mount Baideng for seven days. The chanyu then let him escape; Sima Qian suggests Modu's wife persuaded him. In 198 BCE the Han agreed a peace giving the chanyu a bride, regular gifts of silk, wine and grain, and equal status, a pattern that lasted about sixty years.

events.text: Xiongnu overrun the Yuezhi and Wusun in Gansu and the Tarim Basin
events.detail: Modu followed up his success against China by making the Yuezhi and the Wusun his vassals. In 178 BCE the Xiongnu overran both peoples in Gansu and pushed into the Tarim Basin; according to later accounts, Modu's son Jizhu killed the Yuezhi king and made his skull into a drinking cup. Sources date this blow between 178 and 176 BCE. The Xiongnu now controlled the oasis kingdoms of the Western Regions and their trade routes, and by Modu's death in 174 BCE they were the most powerful of all the nomads bordering China.

events.text: Laoshang Chanyu drives the Yuezhi from their homeland
events.detail: Modu's son Jiyu, who ruled as Laoshang Chanyu from 174 BCE, kept up the pressure on both China and the Yuezhi, raiding within sight of the Han capital Chang'an in 166 and 165 BCE. During the 160s BCE his forces drove the remaining Yuezhi out of Gansu altogether; the sources date this final expulsion variously from c. 165 to 162 BCE. The Greater Yuezhi migrated far to the west, first to the Ili valley and later to Sogdia and Bactria, while the Lesser Yuezhi took refuge in the mountains to the south. The Xiongnu now held the Hexi Corridor without rivals.

events.text: Failed Han ambush at Mayi starts full-scale war
events.detail: For some seventy years the Han had paid gifts under the heqin treaties, yet Xiongnu raids continued, and the ambitious Emperor Wu wanted a decisive blow. In 133 BCE a trader at the border town of Mayi pretended to offer the city to Junchen Chanyu, while about 300,000 Han troops lay in hiding to ambush him. The chanyu grew suspicious at the sight of herds left without herders, captured a Han soldier who revealed the plan, and withdrew before the trap could close. No battle was fought, but the peace was over: raids escalated, and Han began building a cavalry army to strike deep into the steppe.

events.text: Wei Qing retakes the Ordos for Han
events.detail: After full-scale war broke out in 129 BCE, Emperor Wu's generals took the fight to the Xiongnu. In 127 BCE Wei Qing led 40,000 cavalry out of Yunzhong and outflanked the Xiongnu princes of Loufan and Baiyang, retaking full control of the Ordos, the grasslands inside the Yellow River loop that Modu had recovered after Qin's fall. Han settled about 100,000 people there, created the commanderies of Shuofang and Wuyuan, and repaired the old Qin walls. The Xiongnu lost a key base on the edge of the Chinese heartland.

events.text: Huo Qubing defeats the Xiongnu and Han annexes the Hexi Corridor
events.detail: In 121 BCE Emperor Wu twice sent the young general Huo Qubing against the Xiongnu tribes holding the Hexi Corridor, the chain of oases leading west from the Yellow River towards Central Asia. In the spring he fought through five kingdoms in six days and killed nearly 9,000 enemy troops. Fearing punishment from the chanyu after these defeats, the Xiongnu Prince of Hunye surrendered to Han in the autumn, bringing some 40,000 people with him. The Xiongnu lost the whole corridor from Gansu to Lop Nur, which Han organised into commanderies, cutting the Xiongnu off from the Qiang peoples to the south.

events.text: Battle of Mobei drives the Xiongnu from the Gobi
events.detail: After losing the Ordos and Gansu, the chanyu Yizhixie pulled his court north of the Gobi Desert, hoping the barren land would keep the Han out. In 119 BCE Wei Qing and Huo Qubing each led 50,000 cavalry, with many more foot soldiers, across the desert: Wei Qing routed the chanyu's army, while Huo Qubing destroyed the eastern Xiongnu forces. According to official Han reports, the Xiongnu lost 80,000 to 90,000 men, though fewer than 30,000 of the 140,000 Han horses came home. The Xiongnu were driven from the lands south of the Gobi and never again seriously threatened the Han heartland under Emperor Wu.

events.text: Succession war (60–53 BCE) ends with Huhanye submitting to Han
events.detail: When Xulüquanqu Chanyu died in 60 BCE, a distant relative, Woyanqudi, seized power, and the succession broke down into civil war, with as many as five rival chanyus at one point. Huhanye, Xulüquanqu's son, came out on top but was challenged by his own elder brother, Zhizhi. In 53 BCE Huhanye moved south and submitted to Han China, sending a son as hostage, and in 51 BCE he went to Chang'an to pay homage in person. The Xiongnu fell from the Han's equals to an 'outer vassal', and their realm was split between the pro-Han Huhanye and Zhizhi, who withdrew westward.

events.text: Huhanye's rival Zhizhi is killed by a Han army
events.detail: Driven west by his brother's Han-backed power, Zhizhi allied with the Kangju people near Lake Balkhash around 44 BCE and forced them to build him a fortress, probably near Talas in modern Kazakhstan. In 36 BCE the Han deputy commander Chen Tang, forging an order in the name of the ailing Protector-General Gan Yanshou, led an army of Han and allied troops that stormed the fort. Zhizhi was killed and his head was sent to Chang'an. Huhanye was left as the only chanyu, and the Xiongnu remained loyal Han vassals until the upheavals of Wang Mang's reign.

events.text: Confederation splits into Southern (pro-Han) and Northern Xiongnu
events.detail: During the chaos of Wang Mang's reign the Xiongnu under Huduershi regained the Western Regions and stopped paying tribute. But Huduershi broke the custom of passing power to brothers and named his son Punu as heir, angering Bi, the Rizhu King of the Right, who as eldest son of an earlier chanyu had a stronger claim. In 48 CE eight southern tribes with 40,000 to 50,000 fighters broke away and made Bi their chanyu. The Southern Xiongnu soon became Han allies settled along the frontier, while Punu's Northern Xiongnu kept the steppe around the Orkhon.

events.text: Dou Xian's Han army chases the Northern Chanyu into the Altai
events.detail: By the 80s CE the Northern Xiongnu were weakened by famines and locust plagues, and in 87 the rising Xianbei killed their chanyu Youliu. The Han court seized the chance: in 89 the general Dou Xian, brother of the empress dowager, led three columns, including the main army of the Southern Xiongnu, deep into Mongolia. They chased the Northern Chanyu into the Altai Mountains, killing 13,000 and accepting the surrender of some 200,000 people from 81 tribes. Dou Xian carved a victory inscription on Mount Yanran, rediscovered by Mongolian and Chinese scholars in recent years, and the Northern state was broken.

events.text: Northern Chanyu defeated in the Altai Mountains and flees west
events.detail: After the defeat of 89 CE the Northern Chanyu tried to negotiate, but the Southern Xiongnu wanted their rivals destroyed, and Han attacks continued. In February 91 Dou Xian's generals Geng Kui and Ren Shang struck again, defeating the Northern Chanyu in the Altai Mountains, capturing his mother and killing about 5,000 of his men. The chanyu fled west and was never heard of again, and a successor chosen near Lake Barkol was killed in 93. Most of the Northern Xiongnu were absorbed by the Xianbei, who now took over the Mongolian steppe.

name: Kushan Empire
summary: Kujula Kadphises united the Yuezhi tribes of Bactria in the 1st century CE, and his successors pushed into north-western India. Under Kanishka I (c. 127–150) the empire stretched from Central Asia to the Ganges plain, ruled from Purushapura and Mathura and linking the Silk Road, India and Rome. After Vasudeva I (d. c. 225) Sasanian Persia took the west, and the eastern 'Little Kushans' faded under Gupta suzerainty and the Kidarites by c. 375.

events.text: Kujula Kadphises unites the Yuezhi tribes in Bactria
events.detail: In the 2nd century BCE the Yuezhi, nomads from north-western China, had settled in Bactria (northern Afghanistan), where they formed five tribes. In the 1st century CE the Kushan tribe rose above the others, and its leader Kujula Kadphises welded them into one confederation. According to the later Chinese Book of Later Han, he then attacked the Indo-Parthians, took the Kabul region and conquered Gandhara. His dates are uncertain (c. 30–80 CE by one reckoning, c. 40–90 by another), but he counts as the founder of the Kushan Empire, which now reached from Bactria to the Indus.

events.text: Han general Ban Chao repels a Kushan army sent across the Pamirs
events.detail: Han China's general Ban Chao spent decades bringing the oasis kingdoms of the Tarim Basin under Chinese control, and in 84–85 CE the Kushans helped him against rebels around Kashgar and Turpan. In return the Kushan ruler asked for a Han princess as a bride. When the Han court refused, a Kushan army said to number 70,000 crossed the Pamirs to attack Ban Chao, in 90 CE according to most accounts (some say 86). Ban Chao's smaller force held out until the invaders ran short of supplies and withdrew. The Kushans then sent tribute to China, and the Tarim Basin stayed a Han sphere, limiting the empire's growth to the north-east.

events.text: Vima Kadphises expands into north-west India and issues gold coins
events.detail: Vima Kadphises, grandson of the founder Kujula, ruled from about 113 to 127 CE, although other reckonings start his reign as early as c. 95. He pushed Kushan rule deeper into Afghanistan and north-western India, perhaps replacing the Indo-Scythian ruler of Mathura. He was the first Kushan king to strike gold coins, made to the weight standard of Roman coins from gold that came largely through trade with the Roman world. The coins show how rich the empire had grown as a middleman on the Silk Road, and his conquests carried Kushan territory onto the plains of northern India.

events.text: Kanishka I begins his reign; the empire peaks, reaching Pataliputra
events.detail: Kanishka I, son of Vima Kadphises, came to the throne around 127 CE; older scholars put his accession in 78 CE, a date now abandoned. He ruled from two capitals, Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura, and his Rabatak inscription claims cities across the Ganges plain as far as Pataliputra. He replaced Greek with Bactrian as the language of government and became a great patron of Buddhism, which spread from Gandhara towards China along Kushan trade routes. Under him the empire reached its greatest extent, stretching from Central Asia north of the Oxus to the middle Ganges.

events.text: Huvishka consolidates rule, tightening control of Mathura
events.detail: Kanishka's son Huvishka succeeded around 150 CE and ruled for about thirty years. Rather than launching new conquests, he spent his reign consolidating what his father had won, and early on he worked to tighten his grip on Mathura, the empire's great city in northern India. His coins were minted from Balkh in Bactria to Mathura, and his gold coins and amulets have been found as far east as Pataliputra and Bodh Gaya. His largely peaceful reign, sometimes called the golden age of Kushan rule, kept the empire close to its widest extent.

events.text: Vasudeva I, the last great Kushan emperor, comes to the throne
events.detail: Vasudeva I followed Huvishka around 190 CE and is remembered as the last of the 'Great Kushans'. Dated inscriptions show him ruling from at least 191, minting coins at Balkh in Bactria while governing northern India. His name is that of the Hindu god Vasudeva-Krishna, and he was the first Kushan king named after an Indian god, which suggests his centre of power lay in Mathura. During his long reign a new dynasty, the Sasanians, seized power in Persia (224) and began pressing on his north-western lands, the first step towards losing the empire's Bactrian heartland.

events.text: Vasudeva I dies; the empire splits
events.detail: Vasudeva I died around 225 CE by the usual reckoning, although Chinese records of an embassy he sent in 229 suggest he may have lived a few years longer. After him the empire split into a western half in Afghanistan and Bactria and an eastern half based in the Punjab. Neither had the strength of the old empire, and both faced the new Sasanian kings of Persia, who had just overthrown the Parthians. Later Kushan rulers such as Kanishka II held on, but the single empire stretching from the Oxus to the Ganges was gone.

events.text: Sasanians take the western lands and set up the Kushano-Sasanian kingdom
events.detail: The Sasanians, who had replaced the Parthians in Iran in 224, soon turned east. Under Ardashir I (from about 230) and his son Shapur I (240–270) they took Bactria, Sogdiana and Gandhara from the western Kushans, and Shapur's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam claims the 'domain of the Kushans' as far as Peshawar. The conquered lands were ruled by Sasanian governors who called themselves Kushanshah, 'King of the Kushans', and kept issuing Kushan-style coins. The Kushans had lost their homeland north of the Hindu Kush, and what remained of their power was confined to the Punjab.

events.text: Samudragupta brings the Little Kushans under Gupta suzerainty
events.detail: By the 4th century the 'Little Kushans' ruled only a local kingdom in the Punjab, with its capital at Taxila, having lost Mathura and the Ganges lands. In the mid-4th century the Gupta emperor Samudragupta, expanding from the east, claimed them as subordinates. His Allahabad pillar inscription lists the 'Daivaputra-Shahi-Shahanushahi', which many historians read as a garbled form of the Kushan royal titles, among rulers who offered him daughters in marriage and asked to keep governing their own districts. The Kushans still held the Punjab, but now under Gupta overlordship, and the Guptas became the leading power of northern India.

events.text: Kidarites overthrow the remaining Kushan and Kushano-Sasanian rulers
events.detail: In the mid-4th century new nomads, the Kidarites, a Hun people named after their king Kidara, moved south from Central Asia. Around 360–370 CE Kidara overthrew the Kushano-Sasanian governors of Bactria and the remnants of the old Kushan dynasty. The Kidarites presented themselves as heirs of the Kushans, even striking Kushan-style coins, and by about 390–410 they had also moved into north-western India. The Sasanians were pushed back towards Merv, and Kushan rule survived only in small pockets under Gupta and Kidarite overlords.

events.text: Kushan rule fades out as Kidarites and Guptas hold its former lands
events.detail: Historians usually date the end of the Kushan Empire to around 375 CE, though no single event marks it. The last known Little Kushan ruler, Kipunada, issued gold coins in the Punjab around 335–350 and was probably a subject of Samudragupta. After him, coins struck in the Punjab bear the name 'Samudra', and then those of Kidarite kings such as Kidara, who took over the old Kushan territory. The lands the Kushans had once ruled from the Oxus to the Ganges were now divided between the Kidarites in the north-west and the Gupta Empire in the east.

name: Sasanian Empire
summary: Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians in 224 and his son Shapur I humiliated Rome, capturing the emperor Valerian in 260. For four centuries the Sasanians rivalled Rome and Byzantium; Khosrow I (531–579) sacked Antioch and took Yemen, and Khosrow II briefly held the Levant and Egypt. Exhausted by the war of 602–628 and the civil war that followed, the empire fell to the Arab conquests, ending with Yazdegerd III's death in 651.

events.text: Ardashir I defeats Artabanus IV at Hormozdgan, ending Parthian rule
events.detail: In the early 3rd century the Parthian Empire was weakened by a long struggle between the brothers Vologases VI and Artabanus IV. Meanwhile Ardashir, a prince of the Sasanian family in Pars (Persis, south-western Iran), was conquering neighbouring provinces such as Kirman. On 28 April 224 Artabanus finally marched against him and was defeated and killed on the plain of Hormozdgan, whose exact site has never been found. The battle ended almost five centuries of Parthian rule, and Ardashir took the title 'King of Kings', founding a new Persian empire that soon held the Iranian plateau and Mesopotamia.

events.text: Shapur I captures the Roman emperor Valerian at Edessa
events.detail: Shapur I, Ardashir's son, repeatedly invaded Rome's eastern provinces and plundered Antioch in 253 or 256. The ageing emperor Valerian marched east to stop him, and in 260 the two armies met between Carrhae and Edessa (modern Urfa, in Turkey). The Romans were defeated and besieged, and when Valerian tried to negotiate he was captured: the first Roman emperor ever taken prisoner. He died in Persian captivity, while Shapur's troops raided Cilicia and Cappadocia and deported their people. The victory made the Sasanians the equal of Rome and left its eastern frontier open to Persian raids.

events.text: Peace of Nisibis after Narseh's defeat: Rome gains five provinces east of the Tigris
events.detail: In 296 or 297 the Sasanian king Narseh went to war with Rome and at first defeated the Caesar Galerius near Carrhae. In 298, however, Galerius surprised Narseh's camp at Satala in Armenia, capturing his treasury, wives and children, and then marched south to take the Persian capital Ctesiphon. To recover his family, Narseh accepted the terms agreed at Nisibis in 299. Persia handed over five provinces east of the Tigris, recognised the river as the border and gave up control of Iberia in the Caucasus. The frontier held for some forty years, and the Sasanian map shrank back from northern Mesopotamia and Armenia.

events.text: Shapur II repels Emperor Julian's invasion at Ctesiphon
events.detail: In 363 the Roman emperor Julian invaded Persia with a large army and a river fleet, aiming to take the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon and humble Shapur II. He advanced quickly down the Euphrates and won a battle outside Ctesiphon, but the city's defences looked too strong and his northern army never arrived. Julian burned his fleet and marched inland, where Shapur's scorched-earth tactics and constant raids forced a retreat, and Julian died of wounds from a skirmish near Samarra. His successor Jovian bought peace by handing Nisibis, Singara and other frontier lands to Persia and abandoning Armenia, regaining much of what Narseh had lost.

events.text: Peroz I is killed by the Hephthalites
events.detail: By the 5th century the Sasanians' greatest danger lay in the north-east, where the Hephthalites, a Hunnic people, had risen in Bactria in place of the Kidarites. Peroz I (459–484) had already been defeated and captured by them twice. Against the advice of his nobles and priests he launched a third campaign in 484; according to later accounts, the Hephthalite king Akhshunwar dug a hidden trench, and Peroz and much of his army fell into it and were killed. The Hephthalites seized Nishapur, Herat and Merv, and for years Persia paid them tribute, one of the lowest points in the empire's history.

events.text: Khosrow I invades Syria and sacks Antioch
events.detail: Khosrow I (531–579) had made a 'Perpetual Peace' with the Byzantine emperor Justinian in 532, but angered by Byzantium's Arab clients, the Ghassanids, and urged on by envoys from Ostrogothic Italy, he broke it in 540. In May he invaded Byzantine Syria, sacking Sura and Beroea (Aleppo) and taking silver from towns that paid to be spared. In June he reached Antioch, the greatest city of the Roman East; when it refused to pay, he captured and sacked it. Khosrow resettled its captives in a new city near Ctesiphon called 'Khosrow's Better Antioch', and the raid showed that Persia could again strike deep into Roman lands.

events.text: Khosrow I's forces under Vahriz occupy Yemen
events.detail: In the 6th century Yemen, at the southern end of the Red Sea trade routes, was ruled by Ethiopians from the Christian kingdom of Aksum, allies of Byzantium. When an exiled Yemeni prince asked for help, Khosrow I sent the general Wahrez (Vahriz) by sea in about 570 with a small force; the sources give anything from 800 to 7,500 men. Wahrez killed the Aksumite ruler Masruq in battle, took San'a and restored a Himyarite king, Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, as a Persian vassal. After a second invasion in the later 570s Yemen became a Sasanian province, stretching Persian power to the southern tip of Arabia.

events.text: Khosrow II's armies take Jerusalem
events.detail: The Byzantine emperor Maurice had helped Khosrow II regain his throne, so when Maurice was murdered by Phocas in 602, Khosrow declared war, ostensibly to avenge him. In 613 his general Shahrbaraz won victories at Antioch and Caesarea Maritima, and Jewish rebels, long persecuted under Byzantine rule, joined the advance; between 20,000 and 26,000 are said to have fought alongside the Persians. By mid-614 Jerusalem had fallen, after a siege of about three weeks according to one eyewitness account. The Persians carried the True Cross off to Ctesiphon, and with Palestine annexed, Persian rule now reached the Mediterranean coast.

events.text: Alexandria falls; Egypt is taken by 621
events.detail: After taking Syria and Palestine, Khosrow II's armies turned on Egypt, one of the Byzantine Empire's richest provinces. The invasion began in 617 or 618; the governor Nicetas, a cousin of Emperor Heraclius, could not resist and fled to Cyprus. According to the Khuzistan Chronicle, Alexandria was betrayed to the Persians in June 619, and by 621 they securely held the Nile valley. Egypt stayed in Persian hands for about ten years, ruled by Shahrbaraz from Alexandria. It was the first time the Sasanians had ruled Egypt, and with the Levant and parts of Anatolia also theirs, the empire was at its widest.

events.text: Persian and Avar siege of Constantinople fails
events.detail: By 626 the Byzantine emperor Heraclius had been raiding deep into Persian territory for several years, so Khosrow II tried to end the war by striking at Constantinople itself. A Persian army under Shahrbaraz camped at Chalcedon, across the Bosphorus, while the Avars and their Slav allies, perhaps 80,000 strong, attacked the city's land walls from the European side from 29 June. The defenders under Patriarch Sergius and the patrician Bonus held the walls, and on 7 August Byzantine ships destroyed the rafts meant to ferry Persian troops across the strait. The siege collapsed, and its failure saved the Byzantine Empire from collapse.

events.text: Heraclius defeats the Persians at Nineveh
events.detail: Heraclius now carried the war into the heart of Persia. In September 627, allied with Turkic (Göktürk) troops who soon deserted him, he invaded Sasanian Mesopotamia in a risky winter campaign. On 12 December, near the ruins of ancient Nineveh, he met the Persian army of Rhahzadh; after about eight hours of fighting Rhahzadh was dead and his troops fell back. Heraclius plundered Khosrow II's palace at Dastagird, and soon afterwards the Persian army overthrew Khosrow and his son Kavad II sued for peace. The Sasanians gave up their conquests, the frontier returned roughly to where it had been around 590, and Persia slid into civil war.

events.text: Arab armies win at al-Qadisiyyah
events.detail: Exhausted by the long Byzantine war and years of civil war, the Sasanians now faced the armies of the new Islamic state in Arabia, the Rashidun Caliphate. Caliph Umar sent Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas to Iraq with about 30,000 men, and from July 636 they faced a Persian army of perhaps 60,000, with war elephants, at al-Qadisiyyah, south of modern Kufa. In November 636, after several days of fighting, the Persian commander Rustam Farrokhzad was killed and his army collapsed. The defeat left the Sasanians unable to defend Mesopotamia and opened the road to their capital, Ctesiphon.

events.text: Ctesiphon falls to the Arabs
events.detail: After al-Qadisiyyah the Arab army of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas advanced on Ctesiphon, the Persian capital on the Tigris since Parthian times. They besieged it from January to March 637, and when the defenders abandoned the city, King Yazdegerd III had already withdrawn to Hulwan in the Zagros foothills with much of the imperial treasure. Arab columns caught many of the refugees and seized huge booty. The fall of Ctesiphon consolidated Muslim rule over all of Mesopotamia, the empire's richest farmland, and confined the Sasanian state to the Iranian plateau.

events.text: Defeat at Nahavand opens the Iranian plateau to the Arabs
events.detail: Yazdegerd III still hoped to win back Mesopotamia, and gathered a large army in the Zagros Mountains. In 642 (some accounts say December 641) it met the Rashidun army of an-Nu'man ibn Muqarrin near Nahavand in western Iran. The battle was a catastrophic defeat for the Persians and marks the end of organised Sasanian resistance. Isfahan and other cities soon fell, and Yazdegerd escaped to the Merv region but could never raise another large army. The Iranian plateau now lay open, and over the following years the Arabs conquered it province by province.

events.text: Yazdegerd III is murdered near Merv: the empire ends
events.detail: After his defeats Yazdegerd III fled from province to province, through Kirman and Sakastan (Sistan) to Khorasan, hoping to raise new armies; he even asked Tang China for help, without success. He quarrelled with the local governors whose support he needed, and in 651, beaten once more, he took refuge with a miller near Merv. The miller murdered him, either for his jewels or, by another account, on the orders of the governor Mahoe Suri. His death ended the Sasanian dynasty after more than four centuries, and its lands passed to the caliphate, though Tabaristan by the Caspian held out for about a century.

name: Gupta Empire
summary: From the Gangetic plain, Chandragupta I (c. 319–335) raised the Gupta dynasty to imperial rank; Samudragupta's conquests and Chandragupta II's defeat of the Western Satraps made it the dominant power of northern India, a 'Golden Age' of art and science. Skandagupta repelled the Huns c. 455, but after him the empire lost ground to feudatories and to the Alchon Huns under Toramana and Mihirakula, and it had faded by the mid-6th century.

events.text: Chandragupta I raises the dynasty to imperial rank; the Gupta era begins
events.detail: In the early 4th century the Guptas were a minor dynasty in the Ganges plain: the founder Gupta and his son Ghatotkacha were called only 'Maharaja', great king. Chandragupta I took the grander title 'Maharajadhiraja', great king of kings, and issued gold coins. Many historians link his rise to his marriage with the Licchavi princess Kumaradevi, who appears beside him on those coins. His accession is often placed in 319–320, the start of the Gupta era, though who founded that era is uncertain. From its capital at Pataliputra the dynasty now began its rise to imperial power.

events.text: Samudragupta begins the conquests recorded on the Allahabad Pillar
events.detail: Chandragupta I's son Samudragupta took the throne around 335 and turned a regional kingdom into an empire. His courtier Harisena recorded his campaigns in a long inscription added to the Allahabad Pillar, an old pillar of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka. It says he 'uprooted' many kings of the north and annexed their lands, captured and then released kings of the south as far as Kanchipuram, and made frontier kingdoms pay tribute. At its height his direct rule stretched from the Ravi river in Punjab to the Brahmaputra in Assam, and he performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice to proclaim his imperial power.

events.text: Chandragupta II succeeds; Kalidasa at court, Faxian visits
events.detail: Samudragupta's son Chandragupta II, also known as Vikramaditya, became emperor around 375; a later play claims he first had to remove an elder brother, Ramagupta, a story whose truth is disputed. He extended Gupta power by war and by marriage alliances, notably marrying his daughter Prabhavatigupta into the Vakataka dynasty of the Deccan. His reign is remembered as a high point of Gupta culture: the poet Kalidasa may have been his court poet, and the Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Faxian, who spent about six years in the Gupta lands, described them as peaceful and prosperous. Under him the empire reached its height.

events.text: Western Satraps conquered (between c. 397 and 409); Ujjain a second capital
events.detail: For more than two centuries the Western Satraps, Shaka (Indo-Scythian) rulers based at Ujjain, had held Gujarat and western Malwa, with ports such as Barygaza on the Arabian Sea. Chandragupta II campaigned in central India, and the Satraps' coins stop abruptly in the 390s, then reappear dated in the Gupta era, showing that he had conquered them. The exact date is unknown, somewhere between about 397 and 409. The victory carried Gupta rule to the western coast, and according to one theory Ujjain became a second Gupta capital under a royal prince, which may explain later legends of King Vikramaditya ruling there.

events.text: Kumaragupta I succeeds; Nalanda traditionally founded in his reign
events.detail: Chandragupta II's son Kumaragupta I ruled from about 415 to 455 and kept intact an empire reaching from Gujarat in the west to Bengal in the east. Little is known of his wars, but he performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice, a ritual claim to imperial sovereignty. He is usually identified with King Shakraditya, whom a seal found at the site and later Buddhist writers name as the founder of the monastery at Nalanda in Bihar, around 427. Nalanda grew into one of Asia's great centres of Buddhist learning, but late in his reign new enemies, perhaps the Pushyamitras or the Hunas, may already have threatened the empire.

events.text: Skandagupta repels the Hunas (455–457)
events.detail: Around 455 Skandagupta, son of Kumaragupta I, took the throne, possibly after a disputed succession. His Bhitari pillar inscription says he restored 'the fallen fortunes of his family', first against enemies usually read as the Pushyamitras and then in close conflict with the Hunas, probably the Kidarites, who had pushed into north-western India as far as the Indus. The date of the Huna war is uncertain, but his Junagadh inscription of about 457–458 already celebrates victory over foreigners. He kept the empire's inherited lands, though the cost of these wars drained its resources.

events.text: Skandagupta dies; decline sets in
events.detail: Skandagupta's last known date is about 467–468, and he is generally considered the last of the great Gupta emperors. He was probably followed by his half-brother Purugupta and then by a run of short reigns, including Kumaragupta II and Budhagupta. Gupta coins show that the dynasty lost control of much of western India after about 467–469. Former feudatories and provincial rulers grew more independent, and the empire, though still holding the Ganges heartland, was shrinking and weakening just as a new wave of Huna invaders gathered in the north-west.

events.text: Toramana's Alchon Huns push into central India and sack Kausambi
events.detail: The Alchon Huns, one of the Huna peoples from Central Asia, had established themselves in Gandhara and the Punjab. In the late 490s their king Toramana broke through the Gupta defences in the north-west, and much of the empire there was overrun by about 500. His inscriptions show him ruling Malwa and reaching northern Gujarat, and seals bearing his name and the title 'Huna king' found at Kausambi, on the Yamuna, suggest the city was sacked around 497–500, though one seal's authenticity is questioned. The Huns had torn away the empire's western provinces and now threatened its Ganges heartland.

events.text: Battle of Eran (Bhanugupta); Malwa probably falls to Toramana
events.detail: Malwa in central India was a key Gupta province, and at Eran it was held by Bhanugupta, probably a local Gupta ruler or governor. An inscription at Eran, dated to Gupta year 191 (510 CE), records that he fought in 'a great battle' in which the noble Goparaja was killed and his wife burned herself on his funeral pyre, one of the earliest recorded cases of sati. The inscription does not say who the enemy was or who won. Many historians think Bhanugupta was defeated by Toramana and that Malwa passed to the Huns, although others read the battle as a Gupta victory.

events.text: Yashodharman of Malwa defeats the Hun king Mihirakula
events.detail: Toramana's son Mihirakula extended Alchon Hun power across northern India and was remembered, especially by Buddhist writers, for destroying monasteries and killing monks. In 528 he was defeated by Yashodharman, an Aulikara king of Malwa ruling from Dashapura (Mandsaur), possibly together with the Gupta emperor Narasimhagupta. Yashodharman celebrated the victory on pillars at Sondani, near Mandsaur, boasting that even Mihirakula had bowed at his feet. The defeat ended the Alchon Hun era in India, but the winner was a new regional power rather than the Guptas, whose authority kept shrinking.

events.text: Last known Gupta inscription
events.detail: By the 540s the main Gupta line ruled only a reduced kingdom in the east, and Yashodharman of Malwa had occupied most of northern and central India around 532. The last known inscription of a Gupta emperor comes from the reign of Vishnugupta: the Damodarpur copper plate, which records a grant of land in the Kotivarsha district, at modern Bangarh in West Bengal, in 542 or 543. Royal land grants like this show where a king's authority was still recognised, so this one suggests that Gupta rule now survived mainly in the east, in Bengal.

events.text: Gupta rule has effectively ended; northern India fragments
events.detail: Vishnugupta, reigning until about 550, is usually counted as the last recognised ruler of the main Gupta line, though the succession of the 6th-century Guptas is unclear. The empire had been worn down by the Huna invasions, by the rise of former feudatories and rivals such as Yashodharman of Malwa and the Vakatakas, and by the loss of trade and tax revenue. In the Ganges heartland its place was taken by the Maukhari and Pushyabhuti dynasties, who even copied Gupta-style silver coins. Northern India was once again divided among regional kingdoms.
